01_Acids_bases_indicators_and_neutralisa.title: Acids, bases, indicators and neutralisation
01_Acids_bases_indicators_and_neutralisa.subject: Chemistry

objectives.statement: Describe and write word and balanced symbol equations for the reactions of acids with metals, with bases (including alkalis) and with carbonates, and state that an acid-base reaction that produces only a salt and water is a neutralisation.
Use litmus, methyl orange and universal indicator colour changes, together with relative pH values, to classify an unknown solution as acidic, neutral or alkaline.

prerequisites.statement: Write a word equation for a reaction, naming reactants and products in the correct order (reactants on the left, products on the right).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every reaction pattern in this lesson is first stated as a word equation; without a secure grasp of that format, the three acid reaction patterns cannot be told apart or written correctly.

prerequisites.statement: Recognise that a chemical change produces one or more new substances with different properties from the reactants, rather than just mixing them together.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Neutralisation is a genuine chemical change (a new salt and water replace the acid and base); confusing it with simple mixing makes the products of a reaction hard to predict confidently.

diagnostic_items.question: Write the word equation for magnesium reacting with hydrochloric acid, given that the products are magnesium chloride and hydrogen.
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: magnesium + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + hydrogen

common_wrong_answers.answer: hydrochloric acid + magnesium → hydrogen + magnesium chloride
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner has correctly identified the substances but has not noticed that both reactant order and product order are usually written for clarity in the metal-first, salt-first convention used throughout this unit; this is not itself wrong chemistry, but it signals the word-equation format has not been practised consistently.

common_wrong_answers.answer: magnesium + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner has forgotten that a metal reacting with an acid always releases hydrogen gas as a second product, not just the salt.

common_wrong_answers.answer: magnesium + chlorine → magnesium chloride
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner has substituted 'chlorine' for 'hydrochloric acid', confusing the acid (a compound) with the element it contains.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: This checks whether the learner can turn a verbal description into a correctly formatted word equation with reactants and both products named, which every pattern in this lesson depends on.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Underline the reactants and products separately in the original sentence before writing anything, then copy the reactants to the left of an arrow and the products to the right, checking that a metal + acid reaction always lists two products.

diagnostic_items.question: A spatula of black copper(II) oxide powder is stirred into colourless dilute sulfuric acid. The black powder disappears and the liquid turns blue. Is this a chemical change or simply mixing? Give one piece of evidence from the description to support your answer.
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: A chemical change: a new substance with different properties has been made. The blue colour is copper(II) sulfate solution, which is neither the black solid nor the colourless acid that were there at the start.

common_wrong_answers.answer: Simply mixing, because the solid has dissolved in the liquid.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner reads 'the solid disappears' as dissolving and has not used the colour change, which shows a substance with properties neither starting material had.

common_wrong_answers.answer: A chemical change, because the solid disappeared.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The conclusion is right but the evidence is not: a solid also disappears when it simply dissolves, so this observation on its own cannot tell the two apart.

common_wrong_answers.answer: Simply mixing, because no gas was given off.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner treats bubbling as the only possible evidence of a chemical change, instead of accepting a new colour as evidence of a new substance.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: This checks whether the learner judges a chemical change by the appearance of a new substance with different properties rather than by whether the solid 'vanished' - which is exactly how neutralisation is justified in this lesson.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Before deciding, list the properties of what was present at the start and what is present at the end; if any property (colour, state, smell, a gas) belongs to a substance that was not there before, a new substance has formed and the change is chemical.

theory_blocks.title: Chemical character you can actually observe
theory_blocks.body:
An acid or a base is not defined by a label on a bottle; it is defined by how it behaves. Acids share a family of characteristic reactions - with certain metals, with bases, and with carbonates - and they change the colour of certain dyes called indicators in a consistent way.

Before learning any names or equations, the key habit this lesson builds is: look at [[blue:what actually happens]] (bubbles, colour change, heat, a new solid or gas), and use that evidence to decide what kind of substance you are dealing with.

This matters because the same acid can be identified in more than one way: by its reaction with a metal (bubbles of a gas), by its effect on an indicator (a colour), or by its pH (a number).

A confident chemist can move between all three kinds of evidence for the same substance.

theory_blocks.title: Three characteristic acid reactions
theory_blocks.body:
Acids react in three characteristic ways, each with its own recognisable evidence:

1. **Acid + metal** $\rightarrow$ salt + hydrogen. Evidence: bubbles of a gas that gives a 'squeaky pop' with a lit splint. Example: $\mathrm{Mg(s)} + 2\mathrm{HCl(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{MgCl_{2}(aq)} + \mathrm{H_{2}(g)}$.
2. **Acid + base** $\rightarrow$ salt + water. Evidence: the mixture's temperature rises slightly and, if the base is coloured, a colour change happens as it reacts. Example: $2\mathrm{NaOH(aq)} + \mathrm{H_{2}SO_{4}(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Na_{2}SO_{4}(aq)} + 2\mathrm{H_{2}O(l)}$.
3. **Acid + carbonate** $\rightarrow$ salt + water + carbon dioxide. Evidence: vigorous bubbling of a gas that turns limewater milky. Example: $\mathrm{CaCO_{3}(s)} + 2\mathrm{HCl(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{CaCl_{2}(aq)} + \mathrm{H_{2}O(l)} + \mathrm{CO_{2}(g)}$.

In every case, the name of the salt formed combines the metal (or ammonium) from the base/carbonate/metal with the acid's 'anion half': hydrochloric acid gives chlorides, sulfuric acid gives sulfates, nitric acid gives nitrates.

theory_blocks.title: Base and alkali are not the same word
theory_blocks.body:
In this course, a **base** is any metal oxide or metal hydroxide - it reacts with an acid to form a salt and water whether or not it dissolves in water.

An [[blue:**alkali**]] is specifically a base that is soluble in water, so it releases hydroxide ions, $\mathrm{OH^-}$, into solution and can change indicator colour on its own, without even being mixed with an acid yet.

Every alkali is a base (sodium hydroxide, $\mathrm{NaOH}$, is both). But plenty of bases are not alkalis: copper(II) oxide, $\mathrm{CuO}$, is a base - it reacts fully with dilute sulfuric acid to form copper(II) sulfate and water - yet it is insoluble, so a jar of solid $\mathrm{CuO}$ on its own will not turn an indicator any colour at all.

Calling every base 'alkaline' is the single most common slip in this topic; check solubility before assuming it.

theory_blocks.title: Indicators and the pH scale
theory_blocks.body:
An **indicator** is a dye that is one colour in acidic conditions and a different colour in alkaline conditions. Three indicators are used throughout this course:

| Indicator | Colour in acid | Colour in alkali | Colour at neutral |
|---|---|---|---|
| Litmus | red | blue | purple |
| Methyl orange | red | yellow | yellow (it is orange only in the narrow range around pH 3-4) |
| Universal indicator | red (strongly acidic) through orange/yellow (weakly acidic) | blue through purple (strongly alkaline) | green |

The **pH scale** runs from 0 to 14 and gives a number to how acidic or alkaline a solution is: pH below 7 is acidic (the lower the number, the more strongly acidic), pH exactly 7 is neutral, and pH above 7 is alkaline (the higher the number, the more strongly alkaline).

Universal indicator is the only one of the three that gives a full range of colours matched to this scale, which is why it is used whenever a specific pH value, not just 'acid or alkali', needs to be read off.

assets.caption: The pH scale from 0 to 14: red and pink below 7 is acidic, the narrow green band is neutral at pH 7, blue and navy above 7 is alkaline, with two everyday liquids marked for scale.
assets.purpose: Give pH values a fixed visual position relative to the neutral point, so 'how far from 7, and in which direction' becomes a single glance rather than a memorised rule.

theory_blocks.title: Reading indicator colour, pH and products together
A method for predicting and checking the products of an acid reaction
theory_blocks.body:
1. Identify which of the three patterns applies: is the other reactant a metal, a base (oxide/hydroxide), or a carbonate?
2. Name the salt: combine the metal/ammonium ion from the other reactant with the acid's anion (chloride for HCl, sulfate for $\mathrm{H_{2}SO_{4}}$, nitrate for $\mathrm{HNO_{3}}$).
3. List every product for that pattern - metal gives salt + hydrogen; base gives salt + water; carbonate gives salt + water **and** carbon dioxide (never forget the third product here).
4. Write the word equation first, then the correct formula for every substance, then balance using coefficients only, exactly as practised with formulas and equations earlier in the course.
5. Check the balanced equation by counting atoms of every element on both sides before accepting it as the answer.

keywords.definition: A substance that reacts with metals, bases and carbonates in characteristic ways and has a pH below 7 in solution.
A metal oxide or metal hydroxide that reacts with an acid to form a salt and water.
A base that is soluble in water, releasing hydroxide ions into solution.
A dye that changes colour depending on whether the solution it is in is acidic, neutral or alkaline.
A numerical scale from 0 to 14 showing how acidic (below 7) or alkaline (above 7) a solution is, with 7 being neutral.
A reaction between an acid and a base in which the acid is exactly cancelled out, producing a salt and water only.
An ionic compound formed when the hydrogen of an acid is replaced by a metal or ammonium ion.

worked_examples.statement: **A metal reacting with an acid.** Magnesium ribbon is added to dilute hydrochloric acid. Predict the products and write the balanced symbol equation with state symbols.
knowns: Reactants: magnesium (a metal) and hydrochloric acid
unknowns: Name and formula of the salt
reasoning: The other reactant is a metal, so the pattern is acid + metal → salt + hydrogen.
The salt combines magnesium with chloride (from hydrochloric acid): magnesium chloride, $\mathrm{MgCl_{2}}$.

Writing the skeleton equation $\mathrm{Mg} + \mathrm{HCl} \rightarrow \mathrm{MgCl_{2}} + \mathrm{H_{2}}$ and balancing chlorine (2 needed on the left) fixes the HCl coefficient at 2; hydrogen is then already balanced at 2 on each side.
worked_examples.interpretation: Left side: 1 Mg, 2 H, 2 Cl. Right side: 1 Mg, 2 Cl, 2 H. Every element matches, confirming the equation. The bubbling observed is hydrogen gas, which would give a squeaky pop with a lit splint.

worked_examples.statement: **A base reacting with a diprotic acid.** Sodium hydroxide solution is neutralised by dilute sulfuric acid. Predict the products and write the balanced symbol equation with state symbols.
knowns: Reactants: sodium hydroxide (an alkali) and sulfuric acid, $\mathrm{H_{2}SO_{4}}$
unknowns: Name and formula of the salt
Balanced equation, including the correct coefficient of NaOH
reasoning: The other reactant is a base (and an alkali, since it is soluble), so the pattern is acid + base → salt + water.
The salt combines sodium with sulfate (from sulfuric acid): sodium sulfate, $\mathrm{Na_{2}SO_{4}}$, which needs two sodium ions per formula unit.

Skeleton equation $\mathrm{NaOH} + \mathrm{H_{2}SO_{4}} \rightarrow \mathrm{Na_{2}SO_{4}} + \mathrm{H_{2}O}$: sodium needs 2 $\mathrm{NaOH}$ on the left to match $\mathrm{Na_{2}SO_{4}}$,

which then supplies 2 hydrogen and 2 oxygen atoms from the hydroxide groups, exactly matching 2 $\mathrm{H_{2}O}$ on the right together with the hydrogen from the acid.
worked_examples.interpretation: Left side: 2 Na, 2+4=6 O, 2+2=4 H, 1 S. Right side: 2 Na, 1 S, 4+2=6 O, 2×2=4 H. Every element matches. A single acid molecule here needs two formula units of base, because sulfuric acid can donate two hydrogen ions, not one.

worked_examples.statement: **Why a carbonate reaction needs a third product.** Calcium carbonate (marble chips) is added to dilute hydrochloric acid. A student writes the products as 'calcium chloride and water' only. Explain what is missing and give the correct balanced equation.
knowns: Reactants: calcium carbonate and hydrochloric acid
reasoning: The student has applied the acid + base pattern (salt + water only), but calcium carbonate is a carbonate, not a base, so the pattern is acid + carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide.

The vigorous bubbling observed is direct physical evidence of a gas being released, which 'salt + water only' cannot account for; that gas is carbon dioxide, confirmed because it turns limewater milky.

Balancing $\mathrm{CaCO_{3}} + \mathrm{HCl} \rightarrow \mathrm{CaCl_{2}} + \mathrm{H_{2}O} + \mathrm{CO_{2}}$: chlorine needs 2 on the left ($2\mathrm{HCl}$) to match $\mathrm{CaCl_{2}}$;

that also supplies 2 hydrogen atoms, matching 1 $\mathrm{H_{2}O}$; carbon and the remaining oxygen were already balanced by 1 $\mathrm{CO_{2}}$.
worked_examples.interpretation:
Left side: 1 Ca, 1 C, 3 O, 2 H, 2 Cl. Right side: 1 Ca, 2 Cl, 2 H, 1 O (water) + 2 O (carbon dioxide) = 3 O, 1 C. Every acid-carbonate reaction produces this third gaseous product;

leaving it out is never just a simplification, it is a missing product.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Treating a carbonate as if it were a base and stopping at 'salt and water', instead of checking what the observed bubbling is evidence of.

worked_examples.statement: **Combining indicator evidence with a neutralisation calculation (extension: calculations with concentrations in mol/dm3 go beyond the 0654 syllabus).** $25.0\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of $0.40\,\mathrm{mol/dm^3}$ hydrochloric acid exactly neutralises $20.0\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of sodium hydroxide solution of unknown concentration. A few drops of methyl orange are used as the indicator, and the flask contents change sharply from yellow to orange as the last of the alkali is neutralised. Calculate the concentration of the sodium hydroxide solution.
reasoning: Moles of acid used: $n(\mathrm{HCl}) = c \times V = 0.40 \times 0.0250 = 0.0100\,\mathrm{mol}$.
The balanced equation shows a 1:1 mole ratio between HCl and NaOH, so at the exact point of neutralisation $n(\mathrm{NaOH}) = n(\mathrm{HCl}) = 0.0100\,\mathrm{mol}$.
Concentration of NaOH: $c = n / V = 0.0100 / 0.0200 = 0.50\,\mathrm{mol/dm^3}$.
worked_examples.interpretation:
A titration end point needs an indicator with a sharp colour change, so methyl orange (yellow in alkali, red in acid) is used here rather than universal indicator, whose gradual run of colours is ideal for estimating a pH but useless for spotting the exact drop at which the acid is used up.

At that point the flask holds only sodium chloride solution, a neutral salt, so its pH is 7: an indicator colour change and a concentration calculation are two different kinds of evidence for the same event.

guided_exercises.statement: Solid copper(II) oxide, $\mathrm{CuO}$, is added to warm dilute sulfuric acid, where it dissolves and reacts completely. Copper(II) oxide does not dissolve in water on its own. Is copper(II) oxide a base, an alkali, both, or neither? Write the word equation for its reaction with sulfuric acid.
hints: A base is defined by what it reacts with (acids, to form a salt and water); an alkali is a base that specifically dissolves in water.
Does copper(II) oxide dissolve in water by itself? Does it react fully with the acid anyway?
If something reacts with an acid to form a salt and water but does not dissolve in water on its own, it fits one of the two categories but not the other.
guided_exercises.answer: Copper(II) oxide is a base but not an alkali: it reacts with sulfuric acid to form a salt and water (so it is a base), but it does not dissolve in water on its own (so it is not an alkali). Word equation: copper(II) oxide + sulfuric acid → copper(II) sulfate + water.
common_errors: Concluding that CuO 'is not a real base' because it does not dissolve, instead of checking the actual definition of a base against its reaction with the acid.

guided_exercises.statement: A cleaning solution turns universal indicator purple, and a pH meter reads 12. A second, different liquid turns universal indicator pale green, reading pH 7. Classify each liquid (strongly acidic, weakly acidic, neutral, weakly alkaline or strongly alkaline), and state which of the two, if either, must be an alkali rather than just 'a base'.
hints: Match the colour and the pH number to the same region of the pH scale; they should agree with each other.
Remember that pH 7 does not mean 'nothing dissolved' - it means hydrogen and hydroxide ion concentrations are equal.
Only a liquid that is actually dissolved in water and alkaline can be confidently called an alkali from this evidence; a solid base would not show up this way at all.
guided_exercises.answer: The cleaning solution (purple, pH 12) is strongly alkaline; because it is a liquid solution showing alkaline pH directly, it must be an alkali. The second liquid (pale green, pH 7) is neutral - this does not mean it contains nothing dissolved, only that any hydrogen and hydroxide ions present are in balance.
common_errors: Describing the pH 7 liquid as 'not a chemical' or 'just water', rather than recognising that a neutral solution can still contain a dissolved substance.

exercises.statement: Zinc metal is added to dilute sulfuric acid. Predict the products, then write and balance the symbol equation with state symbols.
hints: This is an acid + metal reaction: identify the two products from that pattern before writing any formula.
Sulfate is $\mathrm{SO_{4}^{2-}}$; zinc forms $\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}$, so the salt formula needs no extra subscripts.
exercises.answer: $\mathrm{Zn(s)} + \mathrm{H_{2}SO_{4}(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{ZnSO_{4}(aq)} + \mathrm{H_{2}(g)}$.
exercises.full_solution: Products: zinc sulfate and hydrogen (acid + metal → salt + hydrogen). Zinc forms a 2+ ion and sulfate is 2-, so the salt is simply $\mathrm{ZnSO_{4}}$, and every coefficient in the skeleton equation is already 1. Check: left 1 Zn, 2 H, 1 S, 4 O; right 1 Zn, 1 S, 4 O, 2 H.
common_errors: Forgetting the hydrogen gas product and writing only zinc sulfate as 'the answer'.

exercises.statement: Potassium hydroxide solution is neutralised by dilute nitric acid, $\mathrm{HNO_{3}}$. Write and balance the symbol equation with state symbols.
hints: This is an acid + base reaction; nitric acid is monoprotic (donates one hydrogen ion), unlike sulfuric acid.
Nitrate is a single-charge ion, $\mathrm{NO_{3}^-}$, so check whether more than one formula unit of base is really needed.
exercises.answer: $\mathrm{KOH(aq)} + \mathrm{HNO_{3}(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{KNO_{3}(aq)} + \mathrm{H_{2}O(l)}$.
exercises.full_solution: Products: potassium nitrate and water. Since nitric acid donates only one hydrogen ion, a single KOH is enough: left 1 K, 1 O (from KOH) + 1 H (from KOH) + 1 H + 1 N + 3 O (from HNO3) = 1 K, 1 N, 4 O, 2 H; right 1 K, 1 N, 3 O (nitrate) + 1 O, 2 H (water) = 1 K, 1 N, 4 O, 2 H. Balanced with every coefficient equal to 1.
common_errors: Automatically writing a coefficient of 2 in front of KOH by copying the pattern from sulfuric acid reactions, without checking that nitric acid only needs a 1:1 ratio.

exercises.statement: Sodium carbonate powder is added to dilute sulfuric acid and bubbles are seen immediately. Name all three products, then write and balance the full equation with state symbols.
hints: A carbonate reaction always has three products; the bubbling is evidence for one of them specifically.
Sodium forms a single-charge ion, so check how many sodium atoms $\mathrm{Na_{2}CO_{3}}$ already supplies before adding any coefficients.
exercises.answer: $\mathrm{Na_{2}CO_{3}(s)} + \mathrm{H_{2}SO_{4}(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Na_{2}SO_{4}(aq)} + \mathrm{H_{2}O(l)} + \mathrm{CO_{2}(g)}$.
exercises.full_solution: Products: sodium sulfate, water and carbon dioxide (the gas responsible for the bubbling, confirmed with limewater). Sodium carbonate already supplies 2 Na, so no coefficient is needed on either side: left 2 Na, 1 C, 3 O (carbonate) + 2 H, 1 S, 4 O (acid) = 2 Na, 1 C, 7 O, 2 H, 1 S; right 2 Na, 1 S, 4 O (sulfate) + 2 H, 1 O (water) + 1 C, 2 O (carbon dioxide) = 2 Na, 1 S, 7 O, 2 H, 1 C.
common_errors: Stopping at 'sodium sulfate and water' because that matches the acid + base pattern, and forgetting that a carbonate always adds carbon dioxide as a third product.

exercises.statement: A technician tests an unlabelled colourless liquid. It turns universal indicator red (pH 2); a few drops added to marble chips (calcium carbonate) produce vigorous bubbling of a gas that turns limewater milky; a strip of magnesium ribbon added to a separate sample produces bubbles of a gas that gives a squeaky pop with a lit splint. Identify the general class of substance being tested, then write balanced symbol equations (with state symbols) for both reactions described, assuming the liquid is hydrochloric acid.
hints: Three separate pieces of evidence are given here: a colour/pH reading and two reaction tests. Decide what general class of substance is consistent with all three before writing any equation.
Match each described reaction to one of the three acid reaction patterns before assigning products.
exercises.answer: The liquid is an acid (pH 2, strongly acidic). With marble chips: $\mathrm{CaCO_{3}(s)} + 2\mathrm{HCl(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{CaCl_{2}(aq)} + \mathrm{H_{2}O(l)} + \mathrm{CO_{2}(g)}$. With magnesium: $\mathrm{Mg(s)} + 2\mathrm{HCl(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{MgCl_{2}(aq)} + \mathrm{H_{2}(g)}$.
exercises.full_solution: pH 2 alone already identifies a strongly acidic liquid. The marble chip test (bubbling, gas turns limewater milky) matches the acid + carbonate pattern, giving calcium chloride, water and carbon dioxide. The magnesium test (bubbling, gas gives a squeaky pop) matches the acid + metal pattern, giving magnesium chloride and hydrogen. Both equations balance with a coefficient of 2 in front of HCl, since each product (CaCl2 or MgCl2) needs 2 chloride ions.
common_errors: Using the marble-chip gas test result (carbon dioxide) to try to identify the gas from the magnesium test as well, instead of recognising that each reaction pattern produces its own distinct gas.

exam_questions.statement: (a) Zinc carbonate is added to dilute hydrochloric acid. Write the balanced symbol equation, with state symbols, for this reaction. (b) Describe a simple test that confirms the identity of the gas produced, including the positive result.
hints: This is an acid + carbonate reaction: there are always three products.
The confirming test for this particular gas uses a specific colourless solution, not a lit splint.
exam_questions.answer: (a) $\mathrm{ZnCO_{3}(s)} + 2\mathrm{HCl(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{ZnCl_{2}(aq)} + \mathrm{H_{2}O(l)} + \mathrm{CO_{2}(g)}$. (b) Bubble the gas through limewater (calcium hydroxide solution); if the gas is carbon dioxide, the limewater turns milky/cloudy.
exam_questions.full_solution: Zinc forms a 2+ ion, so $\mathrm{ZnCl_{2}}$ needs 2 chloride ions; balancing chlorine fixes HCl at coefficient 2, which also supplies the 2 hydrogen atoms needed for 1 water molecule. Check: left 1 Zn, 1 C, 3 O, 2 H, 2 Cl; right 1 Zn, 2 Cl, 2 H, 1 O (water) + 1 C, 2 O (carbon dioxide) = 3 O total.
mark_scheme: Correct formulas for all four substances with state symbols (1 mark).
Correctly balanced equation, coefficient 2 on HCl (1 mark).
Names limewater (or calcium hydroxide solution) as the test substance (1 mark).
States the correct positive result: turns milky/cloudy (1 mark).
common_errors: Naming a lit-splint 'squeaky pop' test, which confirms hydrogen, not carbon dioxide; the two gas tests are often swapped by learners.

exam_questions.statement: (Extension: mol/dm3 calculations go beyond the 0654 syllabus.) $30.0\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of $0.20\,\mathrm{mol/dm^3}$ nitric acid is exactly neutralised by $24.0\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of potassium hydroxide solution added from a burette, with methyl orange as the indicator; the flask contents change sharply from red to yellow at the end point. (a) Write the balanced symbol equation for this neutralisation. (b) Calculate the concentration of the potassium hydroxide solution. (c) State the pH of the mixture at the point of exact neutralisation.
hints: Nitric acid is monoprotic, so the mole ratio between acid and base is 1:1.
Convert both volumes from cm3 to dm3 before using $n=cV$.
exam_questions.full_solution: n(HNO3) = 0.20 × 0.0300 = 0.00600 mol. 1:1 ratio, so n(KOH) = 0.00600 mol. c(KOH) = 0.00600 / 0.0240 = 0.25 mol/dm3. Methyl orange is used because it changes colour over a narrow pH range, so the end point is a single clear drop; universal indicator runs gradually through many colours and is used for estimating a pH, not for finding an end point. At exact neutralisation the flask contains only potassium nitrate solution, a neutral salt, so the pH is 7.
mark_scheme: Correct balanced equation with a 1:1 ratio (1 mark).
Correct moles of acid, $n(\mathrm{HNO_{3}}) = 0.00600\,\mathrm{mol}$ (1 mark).
Correct final concentration $c(\mathrm{KOH}) = 0.25\,\mathrm{mol/dm^3}$, with units (1 mark).
States pH 7 for part (c), justified by potassium nitrate being a neutral salt (1 mark).
common_errors: Forgetting to convert cm3 to dm3 before substituting into $n=cV$, giving an answer that is 1000 times too large.

challenge_questions.statement: Four colourless solutions, W, X, Y and Z, are each tested with universal indicator and with litmus. W turns universal indicator orange and litmus red. X turns universal indicator purple and litmus blue. Y turns universal indicator green and litmus purple. Z turns universal indicator red and litmus red. (a) Put W, X, Y and Z in order from the most acidic to the most alkaline, giving an approximate pH for each. (b) State which single piece of evidence separates W from Z, and explain why litmus on its own could not have separated them. (c) A student concludes that Y must be pure water. Explain why that conclusion goes beyond the evidence.
hints: Universal indicator gives a different colour for each region of the pH scale; litmus gives only three outcomes.
For (b), compare what each of the two indicators can actually distinguish.
For (c), think about what a pH 7 reading does, and does not, tell you about what is dissolved.
challenge_questions.answer: (a) Most acidic first: Z (red, about pH 1-2), then W (orange, about pH 4-5), then Y (green, pH 7), then X (purple, about pH 13). (b) Only the universal indicator colour separates them: red shows Z is strongly acidic, while orange shows W is only weakly acidic. Litmus turns red for both, because litmus reports only 'acidic', never how acidic. (c) Green universal indicator shows only that Y is neutral, pH 7. A solution of a neutral salt, such as sodium chloride in water, is also pH 7, so Y could be any neutral solution; the evidence rules out acidic and alkaline, not 'something dissolved'.
challenge_questions.full_solution: (a) The universal indicator colours map straight onto the pH scale: red at the strongly acidic end (about pH 1-2), orange weakly acidic (about pH 4-5), green neutral (pH 7), purple strongly alkaline (about pH 13). The litmus results agree with every one of these - red for the two acidic solutions, purple for the neutral one, blue for the alkaline one - but they add no extra detail. (b) This is exactly the comparison universal indicator is for: it distinguishes relative acidity (how acidic), while litmus distinguishes only the category (acidic, neutral or alkaline). Both W and Z turn litmus red, so litmus alone leaves them tied. (c) pH 7 is a statement about hydrogen and hydroxide ions being in balance, not a statement that nothing is dissolved; sodium chloride solution would give the same green colour and the same purple litmus.
common_errors: Ranking W above Z because 'orange is closer to red than green is', instead of reading each colour off the pH scale in order.
Treating the matching litmus results as independent confirmation of the pH values, when litmus cannot report how acidic or how alkaline a solution is.

mcq.stem: Which statement about bases and alkalis is correct?

options.text: Every base is an alkali, because all bases dissolve in water.
options.why_wrong: many bases, such as copper(II) oxide, do not dissolve in water at all, even though they still react fully with acids.

options.text: Every alkali is a base, but not every base is an alkali.
A base and an alkali are two unrelated classes of substance with no overlap.
options.why_wrong: alkalis are not unrelated to bases; an alkali is defined as a base that happens to be soluble, so the two categories overlap completely for soluble bases.

options.text: Only metal hydroxides can be bases; metal oxides cannot react with acids.
options.why_wrong: metal oxides, such as copper(II) oxide or calcium oxide, are bases and do react fully with acids to form a salt and water.

mcq.explanation: An alkali is specifically defined as a soluble base, so every alkali is automatically a base; but insoluble bases such as copper(II) oxide are bases without being alkalis, so the reverse statement is false.

mcq.stem: A solution of sodium chloride dissolved in water has pH 7. What does this tell you?

options.text: The solution contains no dissolved chemical substance.
options.why_wrong: the solution clearly contains dissolved sodium chloride; pH 7 only describes the hydrogen/hydroxide ion balance, not whether anything is dissolved.

options.text: The solution must be pure water with nothing else present.
options.why_wrong: a solution can contain a dissolved neutral salt and still read pH 7; pH 7 does not mean the liquid is pure water.

options.text: The concentration of hydrogen ions equals the concentration of hydroxide ions in the solution.
The solution is not acidic, alkaline or a chemical at all.
options.why_wrong: it is correct that the solution is neither acidic nor alkaline, but it is still very much a chemical (a salt dissolved in water).

mcq.explanation: pH 7 is a precise statement about the relative concentrations of hydrogen and hydroxide ions being equal; it says nothing about whether any other substance is dissolved in the solution.

mcq.stem: Dilute hydrochloric acid is added to solid calcium carbonate and bubbles appear. Which product list is complete?

options.text: Calcium chloride and water only.
options.why_wrong: this omits carbon dioxide, the gas directly responsible for the bubbling observed; a carbonate reaction always has three products, not two.

options.text: Calcium chloride and hydrogen only.
options.why_wrong: hydrogen is the gas produced when an acid reacts with a metal, not with a carbonate; this reaction produces carbon dioxide instead.

options.text: Calcium carbonate and hydrochloric acid are not able to react at all.
options.why_wrong: this contradicts the bubbling observed, which is direct physical evidence that a reaction is actually taking place.

options.text: Calcium chloride, water and carbon dioxide.

mcq.explanation: Acid + carbonate always gives salt + water + carbon dioxide; the bubbling described is the carbon dioxide gas, which would turn limewater milky if tested.

mcq.stem: Dilute sulfuric acid reacts completely with excess zinc metal. What is the correct name of the salt formed?

options.text: Zinc sulfate
Zinc sulfide
options.why_wrong: sulfate (from sulfuric acid, $\mathrm{SO_{4}^{2-}}$) and sulfide ($\mathrm{S^{2-}}$) are different ions; this reaction involves sulfuric acid, which always gives a sulfate salt, never a sulfide.

options.text: Zinc chloride
options.why_wrong: chloride salts come from hydrochloric acid; this reaction uses sulfuric acid, which gives a sulfate salt instead.

options.text: Zinc hydroxide
options.why_wrong: zinc hydroxide is a base, not a salt, and no hydroxide is involved in this reaction; the salt from an acid + metal reaction always pairs the metal with the acid's anion, here sulfate.

mcq.explanation: Sulfuric acid always produces a sulfate salt; combined with zinc's $\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}$ ion, the product is zinc sulfate, $\mathrm{ZnSO_{4}}$.

mcq.stem: Which row gives the colours of litmus and of methyl orange, first in a dilute acid and then in a dilute alkali?

options.text: In acid: litmus blue, methyl orange yellow. In alkali: litmus red, methyl orange red.
options.why_wrong: the two halves have been swapped: blue litmus and yellow methyl orange are the alkali colours, and red is what both indicators give in acid.

options.text: In acid: litmus red, methyl orange red. In alkali: litmus blue, methyl orange yellow.
In acid: litmus red, methyl orange yellow. In alkali: litmus blue, methyl orange red.
options.why_wrong: the litmus colours are correct, but the methyl orange colours are the wrong way round: methyl orange is red in acid and yellow in alkali.

options.text: In acid: litmus purple, methyl orange orange. In alkali: litmus purple, methyl orange orange.
options.why_wrong: purple is the colour litmus gives in a neutral solution, and methyl orange is orange only in its narrow changeover range around pH 3-4, so neither colour belongs in this row.

mcq.explanation: Litmus is red in acid and blue in alkali (purple when neutral); methyl orange is red in acid and yellow in alkali, passing through orange only in a narrow range around pH 3-4.

flashcards.front: What is an alkali?
flashcards.back: A base that is soluble in water, so it dissolves to release hydroxide ions, $\mathrm{OH^-}$, into solution.

flashcards.front: How does a base differ from an alkali?
flashcards.back: A base is any metal oxide or metal hydroxide and reacts with acids whether or not it dissolves. An alkali is specifically a base that dissolves in water. Every alkali is a base, but not every base is an alkali.

flashcards.front: Does a solution of pH 7 contain no dissolved chemicals?
flashcards.back: No. pH 7 only means the concentration of hydrogen ions equals the concentration of hydroxide ions; a neutral salt solution can still contain plenty of dissolved substance.

flashcards.front: What are the products of acid + metal, acid + base, and acid + carbonate?
flashcards.back: Acid + metal → salt + hydrogen. Acid + base → salt + water. Acid + carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide.

flashcards.front: How do you confirm a gas produced in a reaction is carbon dioxide?
flashcards.back: Bubble it through limewater (calcium hydroxide solution); carbon dioxide turns limewater milky/cloudy.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A base and an alkali are the same thing, so every base dissolves in water and every base solution can be identified by universal indicator turning the solution purple/blue.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Textbook examples of bases reacting with acids very often happen to be soluble hydroxides (NaOH, KOH), so learners generalise from the examples they see most often rather than from the definition.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner calls an insoluble metal oxide, such as copper(II) oxide, 'not a real base' or assumes it must dissolve before it can react with acid.
misconceptions.correct_model: A base is any metal oxide or metal hydroxide; it reacts with acids whether or not it dissolves in water. An alkali is specifically a base that is soluble, so it dissolves to release hydroxide ions into solution. Every alkali is a base, but not every base is an alkali.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask directly: does this base dissolve in water? If yes, it is also an alkali and will change indicator colour on its own; if no, it is still a base and will still react with an acid, but only once it is mixed directly into the acid.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A solution with pH 7 is not really a chemical, or does not contain any dissolved substance, because it is 'just neutral'.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Pure water is the most familiar pH 7 liquid, and learners sometimes equate 'neutral' with 'nothing dissolved' or 'not chemically interesting', rather than with a specific balance of hydrogen and hydroxide ion concentration.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner states that a neutral solution 'has no chemicals in it' or that only acidic or alkaline solutions 'count' as chemistry.
misconceptions.correct_model: pH 7 describes a specific, measurable chemical condition: the concentration of hydrogen ions equals the concentration of hydroxide ions. A neutral solution can still contain dissolved substances (for example, a neutral salt solution); pH 7 is a classification of acidity, not a statement that nothing is dissolved.
misconceptions.remediation: Give a counter-example: a solution of sodium chloride dissolved in water is pH 7 but clearly contains a dissolved chemical. Ask what pH 7 is actually measuring (relative hydrogen/hydroxide ion concentration), not whether anything is present.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: An acid reacting with a carbonate only produces a salt and water, in the same way as an acid reacting with a base.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: The base and carbonate reactions both start 'acid + something ionic' and both produce a salt and water, so the carbonate reaction looks like a copy of the base pattern unless the extra product is specifically checked for.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner writes 'salt + water' as the complete product list for an acid-carbonate reaction, or describes observed bubbling without naming the gas.
misconceptions.correct_model: Acid + carbonate produces three products: a salt, water, and carbon dioxide gas. The bubbling seen in this reaction is direct physical evidence of that third product, and it can be confirmed because carbon dioxide turns limewater milky.
misconceptions.remediation: Whenever bubbling occurs in an acid reaction, ask 'what is this gas, and what test confirms it?' before writing a final product list; for a carbonate, the answer is always carbon dioxide, tested with limewater.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming every base must be soluble and must change indicator colour on its own.
common_mistakes.why: Most classroom examples of bases happen to be soluble alkalis, so the pattern is over-generalised.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Check solubility separately from the definition of a base; an insoluble base still reacts fully with an acid, it just will not show a colour change by itself.

common_mistakes.mistake: Stopping at 'salt and water' for an acid-carbonate reaction.
common_mistakes.why: The acid + carbonate pattern looks like a copy of the acid + base pattern unless the bubbling is specifically linked to a third product.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Whenever bubbling is observed with a carbonate, name carbon dioxide as a product and state the limewater test that confirms it.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating pH 7 as meaning 'no chemical is present'.
common_mistakes.why: Pure water is the most familiar pH 7 example, so 'neutral' gets confused with 'nothing dissolved'.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Remember that pH is a statement about the hydrogen/hydroxide ion balance, not about whether anything is dissolved; a neutral salt solution is still a genuine chemical solution.

common_mistakes.mistake: Extension (beyond the 0654 syllabus): forgetting to convert volumes from cm3 to dm3 before using $n=cV$ in a concentration calculation.
common_mistakes.why: Concentrations are given in mol/dm3 but burette and pipette readings are in cm3, and the unit mismatch is easy to miss under time pressure.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always write the conversion step explicitly (divide the cm3 value by 1000) before substituting into $n=cV$.

exam_notes: When asked for 'the products', list every product the pattern actually gives - a carbonate reaction has three, not two.
A question that gives both a reaction description and a pH/indicator reading expects both pieces of evidence used together, not just one.

Extension (beyond the 0654 syllabus): in a concentration calculation, show the conversion of each volume to dm3 and the $n=cV$ substitution explicitly; method marks are usually attached to these steps, not only to the final number.
When asked to classify a substance as a base or an alkali, state both conclusions explicitly (it is/is not a base; it is/is not an alkali) rather than only answering one of the two.

summary.big_idea: Acids show three characteristic reactions (with metals, bases and carbonates), and indicator colour together with pH gives independent evidence for the same acidic, neutral or alkaline character.
key_points: Acid + metal gives salt + hydrogen; acid + base gives salt + water; acid + carbonate gives salt + water + carbon dioxide - never forget the third product for a carbonate.
A base is any metal oxide/hydroxide; an alkali is specifically a soluble base. Every alkali is a base, but not every base is an alkali.
The pH scale runs 0-14: below 7 is acidic, 7 is neutral, above 7 is alkaline. pH 7 describes equal hydrogen/hydroxide ion concentration, not 'nothing dissolved'.
Litmus, methyl orange and universal indicator each give characteristic colours in acid, alkali and (for litmus and universal indicator) at neutral.
**Extension (beyond the 0654 syllabus).** In a neutralisation calculation using concentrations in mol/dm3, use $n=cV$ and the mole ratio from the balanced equation; always convert cm3 to dm3 first.
formulas: n = c \times V \quad \text{(extension, beyond the 0654 syllabus)}
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Three acid reactions, three product lists - and a carbonate always adds carbon dioxide as a third product, never just 'salt and water'.

epistemic_overrides.note: pH scale is logarithmic — each unit change represents a tenfold change in H+ concentration. This is a key aspect often missed at GCSE.
The pH scale is logarithmic — each unit represents a tenfold change in H⁺ concentration. This is essential for understanding why pH 1 is much more acidic than pH 3, not just "a bit more".

02_Acidic_basic_and_amphoteric_oxides.js.title: Acidic, basic and amphoteric oxides
02_Acidic_basic_and_amphoteric_oxides.js.subject: Chemistry

objectives.statement: Classify stated oxides as acidic or basic from their reaction with an acid or an alkali, and relate the metal/non-metal composition of an oxide to its likely character.
Describe the amphoteric reaction of aluminium oxide and zinc oxide with both an acid and a base, and explain why both reactions, not just one, are needed to establish amphoteric character.

prerequisites.statement: Recall the three characteristic acid reaction patterns from the previous lesson, especially that acid + base → salt + water.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Classifying an oxide depends on recognising whether it is behaving as a base (reacting with acid) in the first place; without that pattern, 'it reacted with acid' has no meaning yet.

prerequisites.statement: Distinguish a metal element from a non-metal element given its name or symbol (from C02: elements and compounds).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The metal/non-metal composition of an oxide is used as a starting heuristic for predicting its likely character, so confusing metals and non-metals undermines that first guess.

diagnostic_items.question: Solid magnesium oxide is added to warm dilute hydrochloric acid and reacts completely. Name the two products and write the word equation for the reaction.
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: The products are magnesium chloride and water. Word equation: magnesium oxide + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + water.

common_wrong_answers.answer: magnesium oxide + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + hydrogen
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner has used the acid + metal pattern instead of the acid + base pattern: magnesium oxide is a base, not a metal, so the second product is water, not hydrogen.

common_wrong_answers.answer: magnesium oxide + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + water + carbon dioxide
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner has used the acid + carbonate pattern; there is no carbonate here, so there is no third product.

common_wrong_answers.answer: magnesium oxide + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner has named the salt but dropped the water, so the acid + base pattern has not been learnt as a complete product list.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: This lesson classifies an oxide by asking whether it reacts with an acid to give a salt and water. A learner who cannot produce that product list has no test to apply, so every classification in the lesson becomes guesswork.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Before writing anything, decide which of the three acid patterns applies (metal, base or carbonate), then write the full product list for that pattern and only afterwards name the salt from the metal and the acid's anion.

diagnostic_items.question: Sort these five elements into metals and non-metals: sodium, sulfur, aluminium, carbon, zinc.
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: Metals: sodium, aluminium, zinc. Non-metals: sulfur, carbon.

common_wrong_answers.answer: Metals: sodium, aluminium, zinc, carbon. Non-metals: sulfur.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Carbon has been placed with the metals, probably because graphite conducts electricity; carbon is a non-metal and its oxides are acidic or neutral.

common_wrong_answers.answer: Metals: sodium, zinc. Non-metals: sulfur, carbon, aluminium.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Aluminium has been treated as a non-metal; it is a metal, and its oxide is the standard amphoteric example in this lesson.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: The metal/non-metal split is the starting heuristic for predicting whether an oxide is likely to be basic or acidic, so a learner who misplaces an element will start every prediction from the wrong guess.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Find each element on the Periodic Table and check which side of the metal/non-metal dividing line it sits on, rather than judging from how the element looks or behaves in everyday use.

theory_blocks.title: An oxide's reactions give away its character
theory_blocks.body:
An oxide is a compound of an element with oxygen. Just like an acid or a base, an oxide's chemical character is not decided by appearance - it is revealed by [[blue:testing it against an acid and against a base]], and seeing which one (or both) it reacts with to form a salt and water.

This is a direct extension of last lesson's acid + base pattern: here, the oxide itself is being tested as the 'base' half of that pattern, and, for a few oxides, also as something that can react with a base in the opposite direction.

theory_blocks.title: Acidic and basic oxides
theory_blocks.body:
A **basic oxide** reacts with an acid to form a salt and water; it does not react with a base.

Metal oxides are usually basic: $\mathrm{CuO(s)} + 2\mathrm{HCl(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{CuCl_{2}(aq)} + \mathrm{H_{2}O(l)}$ and $\mathrm{CaO(s)} + 2\mathrm{HCl(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{CaCl_{2}(aq)} + \mathrm{H_{2}O(l)}$.

An **acidic oxide** reacts with a base (an alkali) to form a salt and water; it does not react with an acid.

Non-metal oxides are usually acidic: $\mathrm{CO_{2}(g)} + 2\mathrm{NaOH(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Na_{2}CO_{3}(aq)} + \mathrm{H_{2}O(l)}$ and $\mathrm{SO_{2}(g)} + 2\mathrm{NaOH(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Na_{2}SO_{3}(aq)} + \mathrm{H_{2}O(l)}$.

'Metal oxides tend to be basic, non-metal oxides tend to be acidic' is a genuinely useful starting pattern - but it is a pattern to test, not a law to apply blindly, as the next section shows.

assets.caption: Oxides of the Period 3 elements from sodium to sulfur: as the elements change from metallic to non-metallic across the period, their oxides change from basic, through amphoteric aluminium oxide, to acidic.
assets.purpose: Tie the metal/non-metal heuristic to a real row of the Periodic Table, so that the amphoteric case is seen as the boundary between the two categories rather than as a random exception to memorise.

theory_blocks.title: A gas 'making' an acid in water is not the same test as classifying the oxide
The two-reaction test for classifying an oxide
theory_blocks.body:
1. Test the oxide with a dilute acid. Does it react to form a salt and water? (Yes $\rightarrow$ it is basic, or possibly amphoteric; No $\rightarrow$ it is acidic, or possibly neutral.)
2. Test the same oxide with a dilute alkali. Does it react to form a salt and water? (Yes $\rightarrow$ it is acidic, or possibly amphoteric; No $\rightarrow$ it is basic, or possibly neutral.)
3. Combine the two results: reacts with acid only $\rightarrow$ **basic**; reacts with base only $\rightarrow$ **acidic**; reacts with both $\rightarrow$ **amphoteric**; reacts with neither $\rightarrow$ **neutral**.
4. One reaction alone is never enough to prove amphoteric character - it only rules out one of the two simple categories. Both reactions must be shown.

| Oxide | Reacts with acid? | Reacts with base? | Classification |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\mathrm{CO_{2}}$ | No | Yes (forms a carbonate + water) | Acidic |
| $\mathrm{SO_{2}}$ | No | Yes (forms a sulfite + water) | Acidic |
| $\mathrm{CuO}$ | Yes (forms a copper salt + water) | No | Basic |
| $\mathrm{CaO}$ | Yes (forms a calcium salt + water) | No | Basic |
| $\mathrm{Al_{2}O_{3}}$ | Yes | Yes | Amphoteric |
| $\mathrm{ZnO}$ | Yes | Yes | Amphoteric |
| $\mathrm{CO}$ | No | No | Neutral |

The $\mathrm{CO}$ row is included as a contrast only: 'neutral oxide' is not one of the categories the 0654 syllabus requires, which asks for acidic, basic and amphoteric oxides.

theory_blocks.title: Oxides as a source of salts
theory_blocks.body:
Every reaction in this lesson that forms a salt and water is, in fact, a preview of the next lesson: a basic or amphoteric oxide reacting with an acid is one of the standard ways to make a soluble salt, especially when the metal itself is too reactive, or the pure metal is not available, to react directly.

Which exact method is used to isolate that salt afterwards - filtering off excess solid, or titrating a soluble alkali - depends on whether the oxide itself dissolves in water, which is exactly the question the next lesson answers.

theory_blocks.title: What the tests actually look like
theory_blocks.body:
Classification is decided by the two reagent tests, but each kind of oxide also has a familiar appearance in the lab.

A basic oxide that is soluble reacts with water to form an alkali: $\mathrm{CaO(s)} + \mathrm{H_{2}O(l)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Ca(OH)_{2}(aq)}$, and $\mathrm{Na_{2}O(s)} + \mathrm{H_{2}O(l)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{NaOH(aq)}$, so the solution turns universal indicator blue or purple.

An acidic oxide that dissolves gives an acidic solution instead: carbon dioxide and sulfur dioxide both turn universal indicator orange or yellow.

| Oxide | In water | In dilute hydrochloric acid | In sodium hydroxide solution |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\mathrm{CaO}$ (basic) | dissolves; universal indicator turns blue/purple | white solid dissolves, colourless solution, no gas | no reaction |
| $\mathrm{CuO}$ (basic) | insoluble, no change | black solid dissolves, blue-green solution, no gas | no reaction |
| $\mathrm{CO_{2}}$ (acidic) | dissolves slightly; universal indicator turns orange/yellow | no reaction | the gas is absorbed, giving a colourless solution |
| $\mathrm{ZnO}$ (amphoteric) | insoluble, no change | white solid dissolves, colourless solution | white solid dissolves, colourless solution |

Notice that [[blue:'no change in water' never rules out a basic oxide]]: copper(II) oxide is firmly basic yet does not dissolve in water at all. Only the test with the acid, and the test with the alkali, settle the classification.

theory_blocks.title: Amphoteric oxides: reacting both ways
theory_blocks.body:
A small number of metal oxides break the simple metal-oxide-is-basic pattern: they are **amphoteric**, meaning they react fully with an acid (like a basic oxide would) **and** fully with a base (like an acidic oxide would), forming a salt and water each time.

At this level, the two named examples are aluminium oxide, $\mathrm{Al_{2}O_{3}}$, and zinc oxide, $\mathrm{ZnO}$.

With an acid: $\mathrm{Al_{2}O_{3}(s)} + 6\mathrm{HCl(aq)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{AlCl_{3}(aq)} + 3\mathrm{H_{2}O(l)}$ and $\mathrm{ZnO(s)} + 2\mathrm{HCl(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{ZnCl_{2}(aq)} + \mathrm{H_{2}O(l)}$.

With a base: $\mathrm{Al_{2}O_{3}(s)} + 2\mathrm{NaOH(aq)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{NaAlO_{2}(aq)} + \mathrm{H_{2}O(l)}$ and $\mathrm{ZnO(s)} + 2\mathrm{NaOH(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Na_{2}ZnO_{2}(aq)} + \mathrm{H_{2}O(l)}$.

An amphoteric oxide is doubly reactive, not inert: it is not 'neutral' in the sense of refusing to react with either reagent.

A genuinely neutral oxide, such as carbon monoxide, $\mathrm{CO}$, is different again - it does not react with an acid or with a base at all.

[[orange:**Not required by 0654.**]] C7.2 asks only that you describe an amphoteric oxide as one that reacts with acids and with bases to produce a salt and water, and that you classify $\mathrm{Al_{2}O_{3}}$ and $\mathrm{ZnO}$ as amphoteric. The names and formulas of the aluminate and zincate salts, the balanced equations for an amphoteric oxide reacting with an alkali, and the 'neutral oxide' category itself are all enrichment here - they make the pattern clearer, but no 0654 question will ask for them.

keywords.definition: An oxide that reacts with an acid, but not with a base, to form a salt and water.
An oxide that reacts with a base, but not with an acid, to form a salt and water.
An oxide that reacts fully with both an acid and a base, forming a salt and water each time.
An oxide that reacts with neither an acid nor a base, such as carbon monoxide. (Enrichment: this category is not required by the 0654 syllabus.)

worked_examples.statement: **Classifying a simple metal oxide.** Copper(II) oxide, a black solid, reacts completely with warm dilute sulfuric acid to form a blue solution and no gas. It does not react at all with sodium hydroxide solution. Classify copper(II) oxide and write the balanced equation for the reaction described.
knowns: Reacts with acid (forms a solution, no gas)
Does not react with a base
reasoning: Reacts with acid only (not with base), so by the two-reaction test, copper(II) oxide is a basic oxide.

The products are copper(II) sulfate (the blue solution) and water: $\mathrm{CuO} + \mathrm{H_{2}SO_{4}} \rightarrow \mathrm{CuSO_{4}} + \mathrm{H_{2}O}$, already balanced with every coefficient equal to 1.
worked_examples.solution: Copper(II) oxide is a basic oxide. $\mathrm{CuO(s)} + \mathrm{H_{2}SO_{4}(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{CuSO_{4}(aq)} + \mathrm{H_{2}O(l)}$
worked_examples.interpretation: Left side: 1 Cu, 5 O (1 from CuO + 4 from H2SO4), 2 H, 1 S. Right side: 1 Cu, 1 S, 4 O (sulfate) + 1 O, 2 H (water) = 5 O, 2 H. Every element matches.

worked_examples.statement: **Classifying a non-metal oxide, and the carbonic-acid trap.** Carbon dioxide gas is bubbled into sodium hydroxide solution and reacts completely to form a colourless solution; it does not react with dilute hydrochloric acid at all. A student argues that, since CO2 dissolved in water forms carbonic acid, CO2 itself must be basic. Classify CO2 correctly and explain what is wrong with the student's reasoning.
knowns: Reacts with a base (NaOH), forms a solution
unknowns: Why the student's reasoning is flawed
reasoning: Reacts with base only, not with acid, so by the two-reaction test, carbon dioxide is an acidic oxide, not basic.

Balancing $\mathrm{CO_{2}} + \mathrm{NaOH} \rightarrow \mathrm{Na_{2}CO_{3}} + \mathrm{H_{2}O}$: sodium carbonate needs 2 sodium, so 2 $\mathrm{NaOH}$ is needed, which also supplies the 2 hydrogen atoms needed for 1 water molecule.

The student's reasoning confuses what CO2 does when classified against acids/bases (the actual test) with what CO2 forms when dissolved in water (a separate fact);

CO2 reacting with NaOH to form a salt and water is the direct evidence that it is acidic, and that is consistent with, not contradicted by, carbonic acid forming in water.
worked_examples.solution: Carbon dioxide is an acidic oxide. $\mathrm{CO_{2}(g)} + 2\mathrm{NaOH(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Na_{2}CO_{3}(aq)} + \mathrm{H_{2}O(l)}$
worked_examples.interpretation:
Left side: 1 C, 2+2=4 O, 2 Na, 2 H. Right side: 2 Na, 1 C, 3 O (carbonate) + 1 O, 2 H (water) = 4 O,

2 H. The classification test (reaction with base, not acid) and the carbonic-acid fact point the same way - both say 'acidic' - they do not contradict each other.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Reasoning that 'CO2 makes an acid, so CO2 must be the opposite (basic)', instead of testing CO2 directly against an acid and a base.

worked_examples.statement: **Why one reaction is not enough to prove amphoteric character.** A student reacts zinc oxide with dilute hydrochloric acid, sees it react completely to form a colourless solution, and concludes 'zinc oxide is a basic oxide'. Explain what further test is needed, carry it out in principle, and state the correct classification.
knowns: ZnO reacts fully with HCl (an acid)
No test with a base has been done yet
unknowns: Whether the student's conclusion is justified
reasoning: Reacting with an acid alone is also exactly what a basic oxide would do, so this single result cannot distinguish 'basic' from 'amphoteric' - the base test has simply not been tried yet.
Testing ZnO with sodium hydroxide solution (a base): it also reacts completely, forming sodium zincate and water, $\mathrm{ZnO} + 2\mathrm{NaOH} \rightarrow \mathrm{Na_{2}ZnO_{2}} + \mathrm{H_{2}O}$.
Since ZnO reacts fully with both the acid and the base, it is amphoteric, not simply basic; the student's conclusion was premature because only one of the two required tests had been carried out.
worked_examples.solution: Zinc oxide is amphoteric. With acid: $\mathrm{ZnO(s)} + 2\mathrm{HCl(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{ZnCl_{2}(aq)} + \mathrm{H_{2}O(l)}$. With base: $\mathrm{ZnO(s)} + 2\mathrm{NaOH(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Na_{2}ZnO_{2}(aq)} + \mathrm{H_{2}O(l)}$.
worked_examples.interpretation: Acid reaction: left 1 Zn, 1 O, 2 H, 2 Cl; right 1 Zn, 2 Cl, 2 H, 1 O. Base reaction: left 1 Zn, 1+2=3 O, 2 Na, 2 H; right 2 Na, 1 Zn, 2+1=3 O, 2 H. Both balance, confirming ZnO genuinely reacts both ways rather than being 'neutral' or inert.

worked_examples.statement: **Aluminium oxide versus a genuinely neutral oxide.** Aluminium oxide reacts fully with dilute sulfuric acid and, separately, fully with sodium hydroxide solution. Carbon monoxide reacts with neither. Write the balanced equation for aluminium oxide with sulfuric acid, and explain why 'reacts with both' and 'reacts with neither' are not the same kind of 'in-between' behaviour.
knowns: Al2O3 reacts fully with H2SO4 and, separately, with NaOH
unknowns: Why amphoteric and neutral are different, despite both being 'exceptions' to a simple acidic/basic split
reasoning:
Balancing $\mathrm{Al_{2}O_{3}} + \mathrm{H_{2}SO_{4}} \rightarrow \mathrm{Al_{2}(SO_{4})_{3}} + \mathrm{H_{2}O}$: aluminium sulfate needs 3 sulfate groups, so 3 $\mathrm{H_{2}SO_{4}}$ are needed;

this supplies 6 hydrogen atoms, matching 3 $\mathrm{H_{2}O}$ on the right, and 2 aluminium atoms are already matched by $\mathrm{Al_{2}O_{3}}$.
Amphoteric (Al2O3) means genuinely reacting with both an acid and a base, producing a real salt and water each time - this is more chemical activity, not less.
Neutral (CO) means reacting with neither, because it has no acidic or basic character to react with an acid or a base at all - this is an absence of this particular kind of reactivity.

Both are 'exceptions' to the simple metal-oxide-basic / non-metal-oxide-acidic pattern, but for opposite reasons: one reacts too much to fit a single category, the other does not react this way at all.
worked_examples.solution: $\mathrm{Al_{2}O_{3}(s)} + 3\mathrm{H_{2}SO_{4}(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Al_{2}(SO_{4})_{3}(aq)} + 3\mathrm{H_{2}O(l)}$. Amphoteric and neutral are opposite kinds of exception: amphoteric reacts with both acid and base; neutral reacts with neither.
worked_examples.interpretation: Left side: 2 Al, 3+12=15 O, 6 H, 3 S. Right side: 2 Al, 3 S, 12 O (sulfate) + 3 O, 6 H (water) = 15 O, 6 H. Balanced, confirming aluminium oxide's acid reaction is a genuine, product-forming reaction, just like its base reaction.

guided_exercises.statement: Sulfur dioxide gas reacts completely with sodium hydroxide solution to form sodium sulfite and water. Predict whether sulfur dioxide reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid, write the balanced equation for its reaction with sodium hydroxide, and classify it.
hints: Sulfur is a non-metal; use that as a starting prediction, but remember it is a heuristic, not a guarantee.
Sodium sulfite is $\mathrm{Na_{2}SO_{3}}$; work out how many sodium atoms that already fixes before balancing.
An oxide that reacts with a base but not an acid falls into which of the four categories from the two-reaction test?
guided_exercises.answer: Sulfur dioxide is predicted not to react with hydrochloric acid (it is a non-metal oxide). $\mathrm{SO_{2}(g)} + 2\mathrm{NaOH(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Na_{2}SO_{3}(aq)} + \mathrm{H_{2}O(l)}$. Classification: acidic oxide.
common_errors: Writing sodium sulfate, $\mathrm{Na_{2}SO_{4}}$, instead of sodium sulfite, $\mathrm{Na_{2}SO_{3}}$, by confusing the product of sulfur dioxide with the product of sulfuric acid.

guided_exercises.statement: An unknown white solid oxide, X, is tested: it reacts completely with dilute hydrochloric acid to form a colourless solution, and it also reacts completely with sodium hydroxide solution to form a different colourless solution. No gas is produced in either test. Classify oxide X, and name one real oxide from this lesson that would give exactly these two results.
hints: Apply the two-reaction test from the theory: what does 'reacts with both' mean for classification?
Check that neither test produced a gas - would a carbonate reacting with acid behave this way?
Only two oxides in this lesson are named as giving both positive results.
guided_exercises.answer: Oxide X is amphoteric, since it reacts fully with both the acid and the base, each time forming a salt and water with no gas released. Zinc oxide (or aluminium oxide) would give exactly this pair of results.
common_errors: Classifying X as 'basic' from the acid result alone, without using the base result that was also given in the question.

exercises.statement: Calcium oxide (quicklime) reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid. Write the balanced equation, with state symbols, and classify calcium oxide.
hints: Calcium forms a 2+ ion; work out how many chloride ions calcium chloride needs.
Check whether calcium oxide is likely to also react with a base, based on the metal/non-metal pattern - this lesson does not give you a reason to doubt that pattern here.
exercises.answer: $\mathrm{CaO(s)} + 2\mathrm{HCl(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{CaCl_{2}(aq)} + \mathrm{H_{2}O(l)}$. Calcium oxide is a basic oxide.
exercises.full_solution: Calcium chloride needs 2 chloride ions, fixing HCl at coefficient 2; that supplies 2 hydrogen atoms, matching 1 water molecule. Check: left 1 Ca, 1 O, 2 H, 2 Cl; right 1 Ca, 2 Cl, 2 H, 1 O.
common_errors: Writing $\mathrm{Ca_{2}Cl}$ or another incorrect formula by not checking that calcium's charge is 2+ before fixing the subscripts.

exercises.statement: Sulfur dioxide gas is bubbled into calcium hydroxide solution (limewater) and reacts completely to form calcium sulfite and water. Write the balanced equation, with state symbols.
hints: Calcium hydroxide is $\mathrm{Ca(OH)_{2}}$; count how many OH groups it already supplies.
Calcium sulfite is $\mathrm{CaSO_{3}}$; check whether any coefficient greater than 1 is actually needed once the formulas are correct.
exercises.answer: $\mathrm{SO_{2}(g)} + \mathrm{Ca(OH)_{2}(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{CaSO_{3}(s)} + \mathrm{H_{2}O(l)}$.
exercises.full_solution: Left side: 1 S, 2 O (from SO2) + 1 Ca, 2 O, 2 H (from Ca(OH)2) = 1 S, 4 O, 1 Ca, 2 H. Right side: 1 Ca, 1 S, 3 O (sulfite) + 1 O, 2 H (water) = 4 O, 2 H. Every coefficient is already 1; no further balancing is needed.
common_errors: Assuming a coefficient of 2 is needed somewhere by analogy with the sodium hydroxide examples, without checking that calcium hydroxide already supplies two hydroxide groups per formula unit.

exercises.statement: Zinc oxide is used in sunscreen and in some ointments. Using two separate reactions, justify why zinc oxide is classified as amphoteric rather than simply basic, and write both balanced equations (with dilute hydrochloric acid, and with sodium hydroxide solution). (Enrichment: 0654 does not require symbol equations for an amphoteric oxide reacting with an alkali, so a word equation would be enough in an exam.)
hints: A justification for 'amphoteric' needs evidence from both reactions, not just one.
Zincate, in $\mathrm{Na_{2}ZnO_{2}}$, pairs one zinc atom with two sodium atoms; check the oxygen count balances once that formula is fixed.
exercises.answer: With acid: $\mathrm{ZnO(s)} + 2\mathrm{HCl(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{ZnCl_{2}(aq)} + \mathrm{H_{2}O(l)}$. With base: $\mathrm{ZnO(s)} + 2\mathrm{NaOH(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Na_{2}ZnO_{2}(aq)} + \mathrm{H_{2}O(l)}$. Because zinc oxide reacts fully with both reagents, each time forming a salt and water, it is amphoteric.
exercises.full_solution: Acid reaction: left 1 Zn, 1 O, 2 H, 2 Cl; right 1 Zn, 2 Cl, 2 H, 1 O - balanced. Base reaction: left 1 Zn, 1+2=3 O, 2 Na, 2 H; right 2 Na, 1 Zn, 2+1=3 O, 2 H - balanced. Both reactions are genuine, product-forming reactions, which is exactly the double evidence amphoteric character requires.
common_errors: Giving only the acid reaction as 'the justification', which on its own would only show zinc oxide behaves like a basic oxide, not that it is amphoteric.

exercises.statement: An oxide of a previously unseen metal, M, is tested in the lab (its formula is not known): it reacts completely with dilute nitric acid to form a colourless solution and, separately, reacts completely with potassium hydroxide solution to form a different colourless solution, with no gas released in either test. Classify MO, write a general word equation for each reaction (using 'M' for the unnamed metal), and state one further piece of information that would be needed to write a correct balanced symbol equation.
hints: Apply the same two-reaction logic used throughout this lesson to a metal you have not been told the identity of.
A balanced symbol equation needs a specific formula for the metal oxide and for the salts formed, which in turn needs the charge of the metal ion.
exercises.answer: The oxide is amphoteric (it reacts fully with both the acid and the base). Word equations: metal oxide + nitric acid → metal nitrate + water; metal oxide + potassium hydroxide → potassium metalate + water. The missing information needed for a balanced symbol equation is the charge of the metal ion M, since that fixes the subscripts in every formula.
exercises.full_solution: The classification follows directly from the two-reaction test: reacts with both acid and base, with no gas, matches the amphoteric pattern exactly (as seen with Al2O3 and ZnO). Writing a balanced symbol equation, however, requires knowing M's ionic charge to deduce the correct formulas (as was needed for $\mathrm{AlCl_{3}}$ versus $\mathrm{ZnCl_{2}}$ earlier in the lesson, which have different subscripts because $\mathrm{Al^{3+}}$ and $\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}$ carry different charges).
common_errors: Attempting to write a specific balanced symbol equation for the oxide without first identifying the metal's charge, and guessing subscripts instead.

exam_questions.statement: Four oxides are tested against dilute hydrochloric acid and against sodium hydroxide solution, with these results: $\mathrm{CO_{2}}$ (no reaction with acid; reacts with base); $\mathrm{CuO}$ (reacts with acid; no reaction with base); $\mathrm{ZnO}$ (reacts with both); $\mathrm{CO}$ (no reaction with either). (a) Classify each oxide. (b) Write a word equation for the reaction of zinc oxide with sodium hydroxide solution, to support your classification of ZnO. (Enrichment: classifying carbon monoxide as a neutral oxide, and writing symbol equations for amphoteric oxides with alkalis, are beyond the 0654 syllabus.)
hints: Use the four-way outcome table from the lesson (acid only / base only / both / neither) for part (a).
For part (b), ZnO's reaction with a base produces sodium zincate.
exam_questions.answer: (a) $\mathrm{CO_{2}}$: acidic. $\mathrm{CuO}$: basic. $\mathrm{ZnO}$: amphoteric. $\mathrm{CO}$: neutral. (b) zinc oxide + sodium hydroxide → sodium zincate + water.
exam_questions.full_solution: Each classification follows directly from the stated acid/base results, matched to the four-category table: acid only is basic, base only is acidic, both is amphoteric, neither is neutral. For (b), an amphoteric oxide reacting with an alkali gives a salt and water, just as it does with an acid; the salt here is sodium zincate, so the word equation is zinc oxide + sodium hydroxide → sodium zincate + water.
mark_scheme: Correctly classifies CO2 as acidic and CuO as basic (1 mark each, 2 marks).
Correctly classifies ZnO as amphoteric (1 mark).
Correctly classifies CO as neutral (1 mark; enrichment - the neutral category is not required by 0654).
Word equation with the correct reactants and products: zinc oxide + sodium hydroxide → sodium zincate + water; accept 'a salt + water' for the products (1 mark).
common_errors: Classifying CO as 'acidic' by assuming any oxide that doesn't react with acid must be acidic, without checking that it also failed to react with the base.

exam_questions.statement: A student tests aluminium oxide only against dilute sulfuric acid, finds that it reacts completely, and concludes 'aluminium oxide is a basic oxide'. Explain two reasons why this conclusion is not fully justified, and describe the further test needed, including its expected result.
hints: One reason concerns what a single positive acid test can and cannot distinguish between.
The further test needed is the same one used throughout this lesson to confirm amphoteric character.
exam_questions.answer: Reason 1: reacting with an acid is exactly what a basic oxide would also do, so this single result cannot distinguish 'basic' from 'amphoteric' - both would give the same positive acid result. Reason 2: aluminium oxide is one of the named exceptions at this level (together with zinc oxide), so assuming it follows the simple metal-oxide-is-basic pattern without testing is exactly the error this lesson warns against. The further test needed: react aluminium oxide with sodium hydroxide solution; it reacts completely to form sodium aluminate and water, confirming amphoteric character.
exam_questions.full_solution: Aluminium oxide with sodium hydroxide: $\mathrm{Al_{2}O_{3}(s)} + 2\mathrm{NaOH(aq)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{NaAlO_{2}(aq)} + \mathrm{H_{2}O(l)}$. Left: 2 Al, 3+2=5 O, 2 Na, 2 H. Right: 2 Na, 2 Al, 4+1=5 O, 2 H - balanced, confirming the base reaction genuinely occurs.
mark_scheme: States that an acid-only test cannot distinguish basic from amphoteric (1 mark).
States that aluminium oxide is a known exception to the simple metal-oxide pattern (1 mark).
Names the base test needed (sodium hydroxide solution, or any alkali) (1 mark).
Gives the correct expected result (reacts fully, forming sodium aluminate and water) (1 mark).
common_errors: Suggesting the further test should repeat the acid test with a different acid, rather than testing with a base, which is the test that would actually distinguish basic from amphoteric.

challenge_questions.statement: Sodium oxide, $\mathrm{Na_{2}O}$, aluminium oxide, $\mathrm{Al_{2}O_{3}}$, and sulfur dioxide, $\mathrm{SO_{2}}$, are oxides of three Period 3 elements. (a) For each oxide, predict whether it reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid, with sodium hydroxide solution, with both, or with neither, and classify it. (b) Explain how the pattern in your answers is linked to the change from metallic to non-metallic character across the period. (c) A student concludes from this pattern that the oxide of any element in the middle of a period must be amphoteric. Give two reasons why that conclusion is not safe.
hints: Sodium and aluminium are metals, sulfur is a non-metal - but one of the three is a named exception to the usual metal-oxide pattern.
For (b), say what changes across the period and what that does to the oxides, rather than listing the three results again.
For (c), think about what evidence is actually needed before any oxide can be called amphoteric, and about where the second named amphoteric oxide of this course sits in the Periodic Table.
challenge_questions.answer: (a) Sodium oxide reacts with the acid only, so it is basic. Aluminium oxide reacts with both, so it is amphoteric. Sulfur dioxide reacts with the alkali only, so it is acidic. (b) Across Period 3 the elements change from metallic (sodium, magnesium) to non-metallic (silicon, phosphorus, sulfur), and their oxides change with them: metal oxides are basic, non-metal oxides are acidic, and the amphoteric oxide of aluminium sits at the boundary between the two. (c) First, amphoteric character can only be established by actually testing the oxide with both an acid and a base; the position of an element is a prediction, never the evidence. Second, zinc oxide is the other amphoteric oxide named in this course, and zinc is a transition element in Period 4, not 'in the middle of a period' in the Period 3 sense - so position does not reliably pick out the amphoteric oxides.
challenge_questions.full_solution: (a) Sodium is a metal and sodium oxide shows no exceptional behaviour, so it behaves as the pattern predicts: it reacts with the acid to give a salt and water and does not react with sodium hydroxide, which is the basic-oxide result. Aluminium is a metal too, but aluminium oxide is one of the two named exceptions: it reacts fully with the acid and fully with the alkali, each time forming a salt and water, which is the amphoteric result. Sulfur is a non-metal, and sulfur dioxide reacts with sodium hydroxide (forming sodium sulfite and water) but not with the acid, the acidic-oxide result. (b) The classification tracks the metallic character of the element, not the oxide's appearance: as metallic character falls away across the period, the oxides stop behaving as bases and start behaving as acids, and aluminium oxide marks the crossover. (c) Two independent reasons: the two-reaction test is the only evidence that establishes amphoteric character, and the other amphoteric oxide required at this level, zinc oxide, does not sit in the middle of Period 3 at all.
common_errors: Classifying aluminium oxide as basic because aluminium is a metal, which is exactly the prediction the lesson warns must be checked by a second test.
Answering (b) by repeating the three results instead of naming the change in metallic character that explains them.

mcq.stem: Sulfur dioxide gas reacts completely with sodium hydroxide solution and does not react with dilute hydrochloric acid. How should sulfur dioxide be classified?

options.text: Basic oxide
options.why_wrong: a basic oxide reacts with an acid, not with a base; sulfur dioxide shows the opposite pattern (reacts with base only).

options.text: Amphoteric oxide
options.why_wrong: an amphoteric oxide reacts with both an acid and a base; sulfur dioxide was only shown to react with the base, not with the acid.

options.text: Acidic oxide
Neutral oxide
options.why_wrong: a neutral oxide reacts with neither reagent; sulfur dioxide does react, with sodium hydroxide.

mcq.explanation: Reacting with a base but not an acid is exactly the acidic-oxide pattern, consistent with sulfur (a non-metal) forming an acidic oxide.

mcq.stem: Which statement about amphoteric oxides is correct?

options.text: An amphoteric oxide is chemically inert and does not react with acids or bases.
options.why_wrong: this describes a neutral oxide, such as carbon monoxide; an amphoteric oxide reacts fully with both an acid and a base, which is more reactivity, not less.

options.text: An amphoteric oxide only reacts with an acid, never with a base.
options.why_wrong: reacting only with an acid, and not with a base, is the definition of a basic oxide, not an amphoteric one.

options.text: An amphoteric oxide reacts with an acid to form a gas, not a salt.
options.why_wrong: an amphoteric oxide's reaction with an acid forms a salt and water, the same product pattern as a basic oxide reacting with an acid; no gas is produced.

options.text: An amphoteric oxide reacts fully with both an acid and a base, forming a salt and water each time.

mcq.explanation: Amphoteric character means reacting completely with both an acid and a base, each time producing a genuine salt-and-water reaction; it is not a form of unreactivity.

mcq.stem: Carbon dioxide dissolves in water to form carbonic acid, a weak acid. What does this tell you about the classification of carbon dioxide as an oxide?

options.text: It is consistent with carbon dioxide being an acidic oxide, which is confirmed separately by its reaction with sodium hydroxide.
It proves carbon dioxide must be a basic oxide, since it produces an acid.
options.why_wrong: forming an acid in water does not make the original oxide basic; carbon dioxide's classification comes from testing it directly against an acid and a base, and it reacts with the base, not the acid, which is the acidic-oxide pattern.

options.text: It proves carbon dioxide is amphoteric.
options.why_wrong: amphoteric character requires a positive reaction with both an acid and a base; carbon dioxide does not react with an acid at all, so it cannot be amphoteric.

options.text: It is irrelevant to carbon dioxide's classification, which depends only on whether carbon is a metal or non-metal.
options.why_wrong: the metal/non-metal pattern is only a starting heuristic; the actual classification still depends on testing the oxide against an acid and a base, as option A correctly states.
