04_Precipitating_insoluble_salts.json.title: Precipitating insoluble salts
04_Precipitating_insoluble_salts.json.subject: Chemistry

objectives.statement: Describe how two soluble solutions are mixed to form an insoluble salt by precipitation, given solubility data, and write the balanced equation for the reaction.

Describe the filtering, washing and drying steps that isolate a pure, dry precipitate, correctly identifying the precipitate as the residue rather than the filtrate, and calculate the mass of precipitate formed from the mass of the reactant that is not in excess (versions that start from a solution concentration in mol/dm3 are extension, beyond the 0654 syllabus).

prerequisites.statement: Filter a mixture and name a soluble salt from the ions it contains (from an earlier lesson: filtration and salt naming).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Precipitation also ends in a filtration step, and naming salts correctly from their ions is needed to predict the two products of a precipitation reaction before any filtering can be planned.

prerequisites.statement: Use given solubility information for a specific substance, rather than a memorised general solubility rule.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: This lesson deliberately supplies solubility data for each solution and product used, rather than requiring a general rule, so learners need to be comfortable reading and using that data directly.

diagnostic_items.question: A mixture of sand and sodium chloride solution is poured into a filter funnel lined with filter paper. Using the words **residue** and **filtrate**, state what is left on the filter paper and what collects in the beaker below.
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: The sand is the residue, left on the filter paper; the sodium chloride solution passes through and collects in the beaker as the filtrate.

common_wrong_answers.answer: The sodium chloride is the residue and the sand is the filtrate.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The two words have simply been swapped: the residue is always the solid caught on the paper, the filtrate always the liquid that passes through.

common_wrong_answers.answer: Both the sand and the sodium chloride are left on the filter paper.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner thinks filter paper stops every solid, including a dissolved one; a substance that has dissolved travels through the paper with the water.

common_wrong_answers.answer: The sand is the residue and the filtrate is pure water.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner has forgotten that the dissolved sodium chloride is still in the filtrate; filtration separates an undissolved solid from a liquid, but never a dissolved solid from its solvent.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Every precipitation preparation in this lesson ends with exactly this filtration step, so a learner who swaps residue and filtrate will look for the insoluble salt in the wrong place throughout.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Ask one question about each substance: does it dissolve in water? If it does not, it cannot pass through the paper and must be the residue; if it does, it travels through with the water into the filtrate.

diagnostic_items.question: Name the salt made of barium ions, $\mathrm{Ba^{2+}}$, and sulfate ions, $\mathrm{SO_{4}^{2-}}$, and give its formula.

common_wrong_answers.answer: Barium sulfide, $\mathrm{BaS}$
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The sulfate ion, $\mathrm{SO_{4}^{2-}}$, has been read as the sulfide ion, $\mathrm{S^{2-}}$; a sulfate keeps all four oxygen atoms in the formula.

common_wrong_answers.answer: $\mathrm{Ba_{2}SO_{4}}$
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The charges have not been balanced: one $2+$ ion is already matched exactly by one $2-$ ion, so neither formula needs a subscript outside it.

common_wrong_answers.answer: Sulfate barium, $\mathrm{SO_{4}Ba}$
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The order has been reversed: the positive metal ion is always named and written first in a salt.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Predicting the two products of a precipitation reaction, and then deciding which of them is the insoluble one, begins with naming a salt correctly from the pair of ions that make it.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Write the two ions with their charges side by side, name the positive one first, then choose the smallest whole numbers of each that make the charges cancel: one $\mathrm{Ba^{2+}}$ with one $\mathrm{SO_{4}^{2-}}$ gives $\mathrm{BaSO_{4}}$.

theory_blocks.title: Two solutions that don't want to share ions
theory_blocks.body:
So far, every salt in this unit has stayed dissolved once it formed. Precipitation is different: two separate, clear solutions are mixed, and the ions they contain combine into a new compound that is insoluble - a solid, called a [[blue:**precipitate**]], appears immediately, right there in the mixture, without any heating or evaporation at all.

This only works when the *product* is insoluble, even though both starting solutions were soluble; the insoluble product is what gets isolated, and everything else stays dissolved.

theory_blocks.title: Choosing the two solutions: supplied data, not a general rule
theory_blocks.body:
To precipitate a chosen insoluble salt, two soluble solutions are picked that together supply exactly the two ions needed - one solution provides the metal ion, the other provides the non-metal (or polyatomic) ion.

No general solubility rule needs to be memorised for this: the solubility of each solution and of the expected product is simply given, since different syllabuses and textbooks state solubility data slightly differently.

For example, to make insoluble barium sulfate, $\mathrm{BaSO_{4}}$, a soluble barium solution (barium chloride) is mixed with a soluble sulfate solution (sodium sulfate): $\mathrm{BaCl_{2}(aq)} + \mathrm{Na_{2}SO_{4}(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{BaSO_{4}(s)} + 2\mathrm{NaCl(aq)}$.

The desired product, $\mathrm{BaSO_{4}}$, is the insoluble one; the by-product, sodium chloride, stays dissolved.

theory_blocks.title: Isolating the precipitate: filter, wash, dry
theory_blocks.body:
1. **Filter** the mixture through filter paper in a funnel. The insoluble precipitate is caught on the paper as the **residue**; the liquid that passes through, the **filtrate**, contains only the dissolved by-product(s), never the precipitate itself.
2. **Wash** the residue with a small volume of distilled water, poured gently over it while still on the filter paper. This rinses away any soluble by-product solution clinging to the surface of the precipitate, without using so much water that any of the (insoluble) precipitate itself would be at risk of being disturbed or carried through.
3. **Dry** the washed residue, either in a warm oven at a gentle temperature or by pressing it between sheets of filter paper, to remove the remaining surface water and leave a pure, dry solid.

No evaporation step is involved anywhere in this method: the precipitate is already solid from the moment the two solutions are mixed, so the task is to separate and clean it, not to concentrate a solution.

assets.caption: Filtration apparatus for isolating a precipitate: the funnel and filter paper hold the insoluble residue, while the filtrate (dissolved by-products) collects in the flask below.
assets.purpose: Make the physical location of the residue (on the paper) and the filtrate (in the flask below) directly visible, so the two cannot be confused in writing.

theory_blocks.title: Writing the equation and predicting the mass of precipitate
theory_blocks.body:
The balanced equation for a precipitation reaction follows the same double-replacement pattern every time: $\mathrm{AB(aq)} + \mathrm{CD(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{AD(s)} + \mathrm{CB(aq)}$, where $\mathrm{AD}$ is the insoluble product.

Once the equation is balanced, the expected mass of precipitate is found exactly as in any other reacting-mass calculation: find the moles of the reactant that is **not** in excess,

use the mole ratio from the balanced equation to find the moles of precipitate, then multiply by its molar mass.

For example, $2.08\,\mathrm{g}$ of barium chloride is dissolved in distilled water and mixed with an excess of sodium sulfate solution. $M(\mathrm{BaCl_{2}}) = 137+2(35.5) = 208$ and $M(\mathrm{BaSO_{4}}) = 137+32+4(16) = 233$, so $n(\mathrm{BaCl_{2}}) = 2.08/208 = 0.0100\,\mathrm{mol}$;

by the 1:1 ratio between $\mathrm{BaCl_{2}}$ and $\mathrm{BaSO_{4}}$, $n(\mathrm{BaSO_{4}}) = 0.0100\,\mathrm{mol}$, and the mass of precipitate is $0.0100\times233 = 2.33\,\mathrm{g}$.

[[orange:**Extension (beyond the 0654 syllabus).**]] The same calculation is often set with the limiting reactant given as a volume of solution and a concentration in $\mathrm{mol/dm^3}$, using $n = c \times V$ with $V$ in $\mathrm{dm^3}$. Concentration in $\mathrm{mol/dm^3}$ is not used anywhere in 0654 - the syllabus states concentration in $\mathrm{g/dm^3}$ only - so treat this version as useful extra practice rather than examinable material. For example, $25.0\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of $0.200\,\mathrm{mol/dm^3}$ barium chloride solution gives $n(\mathrm{BaCl_{2}}) = 0.200\times0.0250 = 0.00500\,\mathrm{mol}$, and so $0.00500\times233 = 1.17\,\mathrm{g}$ of $\mathrm{BaSO_{4}}$ (to 3 s.f.).

theory_blocks.title: Precipitation is not titration
theory_blocks.body:
Titration (from the previous lesson) measures an *exact* neutralising volume, using an indicator colour change as a precise end-point signal, because the product needs to stay dissolved and the two reactants need to be matched exactly.

Precipitation does not work this way: the solid product appears visibly on its own as soon as enough of both ions are present, with no colour-change end point to look for and no requirement to match volumes exactly.

In fact, one of the two solutions is often deliberately used in [[blue:**excess**]], simply to make sure as much of the desired insoluble product forms as possible;

the excess of that reactant then simply stays dissolved in the filtrate, causing no problem at all for the solid product.

theory_blocks.title: Three routes of salt preparation, one unit
theory_blocks.body:
This unit now has three preparation routes, each matched to a specific situation: titration (soluble reactant, soluble product, exact volumes matter), excess solid plus filtration and crystallisation (insoluble reactant, soluble product, evaporation needed), and precipitation plus filtration, washing and drying (soluble reactants, insoluble product, no evaporation at all).

Recognising which family a described preparation belongs to - from whether the reactants and the product are each soluble or insoluble - is the single skill that ties the whole unit together.

keywords.definition: An insoluble solid that forms immediately when two solutions are mixed and their ions combine.
A reaction between two soluble solutions that forms an insoluble solid product.
The solid caught on filter paper during filtration.
The liquid that passes through filter paper during filtration, containing only dissolved substances.
An amount of one reactant greater than needed, added to ensure the other reactant reacts as completely as possible.

worked_examples.statement: **Identifying a precipitation pair.** Lead(II) nitrate solution (soluble) and potassium iodide solution (soluble) are mixed. The product lead(II) iodide is insoluble; potassium nitrate is soluble. Predict what is observed, and write the balanced symbol equation with state symbols.
knowns: Lead(II) iodide is insoluble; potassium nitrate is soluble
reasoning: Since lead(II) iodide is insoluble, it will appear immediately as a solid precipitate as soon as the two solutions are mixed; potassium nitrate stays dissolved.
Lead forms a 2+ ion and iodide is 1-, so lead(II) iodide needs two iodide ions: $\mathrm{PbI_{2}}$; this fixes the KI coefficient at 2 and, matching potassium, the KNO3 coefficient at 2 as well.
worked_examples.solution: A yellow solid precipitate (lead(II) iodide) forms immediately. $\mathrm{Pb(NO_{3})_{2}(aq)} + 2\mathrm{KI(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{PbI_{2}(s)} + 2\mathrm{KNO_{3}(aq)}$
worked_examples.interpretation: Left side: 1 Pb, 2 N, 6 O, 2 K, 2 I. Right side: 1 Pb, 2 I, 2 K, 2 N, 6 O. Every element matches; the state symbols show the solid forming directly from two aqueous solutions, with no gas and no evaporation involved.

worked_examples.statement: **Full mass-of-precipitate calculation (extension - beyond the 0654 syllabus, which does not use concentration in $\mathrm{mol/dm^3}$).** $25.0\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of $0.200\,\mathrm{mol/dm^3}$ barium chloride solution is mixed with an excess of sodium sulfate solution. Calculate the mass of barium sulfate precipitate formed ($M(\mathrm{BaSO_{4}}) = 233$).
knowns: $\mathrm{BaCl_{2}(aq)} + \mathrm{Na_{2}SO_{4}(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{BaSO_{4}(s)} + 2\mathrm{NaCl(aq)}$, a 1:1 ratio between BaCl2 and BaSO4
reasoning: Since sodium sulfate is in excess, barium chloride is the limiting reagent, and its moles determine the amount of precipitate formed.
By the 1:1 ratio, $n(\mathrm{BaSO_{4}}) = 0.00500\,\mathrm{mol}$, so mass $= 0.00500 \times 233 = 1.17\,\mathrm{g}$ (3 s.f.).
worked_examples.interpretation: Using excess sodium sulfate guarantees essentially all the barium ion is precipitated; the calculation uses only the moles of the limiting reactant (barium chloride), exactly as in the excess-solid calculations from the previous lesson.

worked_examples.statement: **Why using excess sodium sulfate is good practice, not sloppy technique.** In the barium sulfate example above, explain why sodium sulfate is deliberately added in excess rather than in a precisely matched volume, and why this does not cause a problem with the purity of the final dried precipitate.
knowns: Sodium sulfate is added in excess, not an exactly matched amount
Sodium chloride (the by-product) and any excess sodium sulfate both remain dissolved
unknowns: Why excess is used on purpose
Why it does not spoil the product's purity
reasoning:
Unlike titration, precipitation has no indicator end point to aim for, so there is no practical way to add 'exactly the right amount' of the second solution even if it were wanted;

using a clear excess instead guarantees that essentially all of the limiting reactant (barium chloride here) is converted to precipitate.
The excess sodium sulfate, together with the sodium chloride by-product, simply remains dissolved in the filtrate; neither one is part of the solid residue.

Washing the filtered residue with a little distilled water removes any trace of this dissolved excess solution clinging to the surface of the solid, so the final dried precipitate is pure barium sulfate, not contaminated by the excess reagent.
worked_examples.solution:
Excess sodium sulfate is used to maximise the amount of barium sulfate precipitated, since there is no indicator end point to match volumes exactly;

the excess stays dissolved in the filtrate (removed by filtering and washing), so it does not contaminate the dried precipitate.
worked_examples.interpretation:
This is the opposite situation to titration, where using 'too much' acid or alkali would ruin the result;

here, using 'too much' of one solution is the normal, correct technique precisely because the product is removed by filtration rather than by matching an exact volume.

worked_examples.statement: **Full procedure and mass calculation.** $30.0\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of $0.100\,\mathrm{mol/dm^3}$ silver nitrate solution is mixed with an excess of sodium chloride solution. (a) Write the balanced equation. (b) Calculate the mass of silver chloride precipitate formed ($M(\mathrm{AgCl}) = 143.5$). (c) Describe how the pure, dry precipitate is obtained from the mixture, naming which part is the residue and which is the filtrate. **Part (b) is extension: concentration in $\mathrm{mol/dm^3}$ is beyond the 0654 syllabus. Parts (a) and (c) are the examinable content.**
knowns: AgCl is insoluble; NaNO3 is soluble
reasoning: $\mathrm{AgNO_{3}(aq)} + \mathrm{NaCl(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{AgCl(s)} + \mathrm{NaNO_{3}(aq)}$, already balanced 1:1:1:1.
$n(\mathrm{AgNO_{3}}) = 0.100 \times 0.0300 = 0.00300\,\mathrm{mol}$; by the 1:1 ratio, $n(\mathrm{AgCl}) = 0.00300\,\mathrm{mol}$; mass $= 0.00300 \times 143.5 = 0.431\,\mathrm{g}$ (3 s.f.).

The mixture is filtered: the insoluble AgCl is caught on the filter paper as the residue; the filtrate (passing through) contains dissolved sodium nitrate and the excess sodium chloride.

The residue is then washed with a little distilled water and dried.
worked_examples.solution:
(a) $\mathrm{AgNO_{3}(aq)} + \mathrm{NaCl(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{AgCl(s)} + \mathrm{NaNO_{3}(aq)}$. (b) Mass of $\mathrm{AgCl} = 0.431\,\mathrm{g}$. (c) Filter: AgCl is the residue on the paper;

the filtrate contains the dissolved by-product and excess reagent. Wash the residue with a little distilled water, then dry it.
worked_examples.interpretation:
The calculation again uses only the moles of the reagent that is not in excess (silver nitrate);

the procedure explicitly separates 'what is the solid' (AgCl, the residue) from 'what is dissolved' (everything else, the filtrate), directly addressing the most common mix-up in this topic.

guided_exercises.statement: **Extension (beyond the 0654 syllabus, which does not use concentration in $\mathrm{mol/dm^3}$).** $25.0\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of $0.50\,\mathrm{mol/dm^3}$ lead(II) nitrate solution is mixed with an excess of potassium iodide solution. Calculate the mass of lead(II) iodide precipitate formed ($M(\mathrm{PbI_{2}}) = 461$).
hints: Write the balanced equation first: $\mathrm{Pb(NO_{3})_{2}(aq)} + 2\mathrm{KI(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{PbI_{2}(s)} + 2\mathrm{KNO_{3}(aq)}$, and check the mole ratio between $\mathrm{Pb(NO_{3})_{2}}$ and $\mathrm{PbI_{2}}$ specifically.
Since potassium iodide is in excess, which reagent's moles should be used to find the moles of precipitate?
Convert the given volume to dm3 and use $n=cV$ before multiplying by the molar mass.
common_errors: Using a 1:2 ratio instead of 1:1 between $\mathrm{Pb(NO_{3})_{2}}$ and $\mathrm{PbI_{2}}$, confusing the KI coefficient (2) with the mole ratio that actually matters for this calculation.
guided_exercises.full_solution: Convert $25.0\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ to $0.0250\,\mathrm{dm^3}$. Then $n(\mathrm{Pb(NO_3)_2})=cV=0.50\times0.0250=0.0125\,\mathrm{mol}$. The equation gives a 1:1 ratio, so $n(\mathrm{PbI_2})=0.0125\,\mathrm{mol}$. Therefore $m=nM=0.0125\times461=5.76\,\mathrm{g}$ (3 s.f.).

guided_exercises.statement: After filtering a mixture of two solutions that formed an insoluble white precipitate, where is the desired solid actually located - in the filtrate, or on the filter paper (the residue)? Explain your answer, and state the next two steps needed to obtain it pure and dry.
hints: Think about whether an insoluble solid can physically pass through the tiny holes in filter paper.
The filtrate is defined as the liquid that passes through; the residue is defined as whatever is caught on the paper.
Two more steps are needed after filtering, before the solid can be called pure and dry.
guided_exercises.answer: The desired solid is the residue, caught on the filter paper - it cannot be in the filtrate, because an insoluble solid cannot pass through the paper. The next two steps are: wash the residue with a little distilled water (to remove any soluble by-product solution clinging to its surface), then dry it (in a warm oven or between filter papers).
common_errors: Describing the filtrate as containing the precipitate, when by definition only dissolved substances pass through into the filtrate.

exercises.statement: $20.0\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of $0.25\,\mathrm{mol/dm^3}$ calcium chloride solution is mixed with an excess of sodium carbonate solution. Calcium carbonate is insoluble; sodium chloride is soluble. Write the balanced equation and calculate the mass of calcium carbonate precipitate formed ($M(\mathrm{CaCO_{3}}) = 100$). (The balanced equation is examinable content; the mass calculation from a concentration in $\mathrm{mol/dm^3}$ is extension, beyond the 0654 syllabus.)
hints: Calcium forms a 2+ ion and carbonate is 2-, so check whether the salt formulas need any extra subscripts.
Use the moles of calcium chloride (the reagent not in excess) to find the moles of precipitate.
exercises.answer: $\mathrm{CaCl_{2}(aq)} + \mathrm{Na_{2}CO_{3}(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{CaCO_{3}(s)} + 2\mathrm{NaCl(aq)}$. Mass of $\mathrm{CaCO_{3}}$ precipitate $= 0.500\,\mathrm{g}$.
exercises.full_solution: Calcium and carbonate ions are both doubly charged, so the formulas need no extra subscripts beyond 1:1, but sodium (singly charged) needs 2 to balance the chloride and carbonate groups: left 1 Ca, 2 Cl, 2 Na, 1 C, 3 O; right 1 Ca, 1 C, 3 O, 2 Na, 2 Cl. $n(\mathrm{CaCl_{2}}) = 0.25\times0.0200=0.00500\,\mathrm{mol}$; by the 1:1 ratio, $n(\mathrm{CaCO_{3}})=0.00500\,\mathrm{mol}$; mass $=0.00500\times100=0.500\,\mathrm{g}$.
common_errors: Using the volume or concentration of the excess sodium carbonate solution instead of the calcium chloride solution to calculate the moles of precipitate.

exercises.statement: Explain why the precipitate is washed with a small volume of distilled water, rather than with a large volume, and why it is not washed using the original reacting solution.
hints: Think about what a large volume of any liquid might do to a fine solid sitting loosely on filter paper.
Think about what is dissolved in the original reacting solution, compared with what is dissolved in pure distilled water.
exercises.answer: A small volume of distilled water is used so that it rinses away the soluble by-product solution clinging to the surface of the precipitate without disturbing or washing away any of the solid itself, and without dissolving any extra impurity into the residue. The original reacting solution is not used for washing because it already contains the dissolved by-products (and possibly excess reagent) that washing is specifically meant to remove.
exercises.full_solution: Distilled water contains nothing dissolved in it, so it can only remove existing impurities from the surface of the residue, never add new ones; using a small volume limits how much of the fine solid could be carried away with the liquid. Using the original reacting solution instead would simply reapply the very substances that need to be washed off.
common_errors: Suggesting the residue should be washed with more of the same solution used to make it, rather than with plain distilled water.

exercises.statement: $40.0\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of $0.125\,\mathrm{mol/dm^3}$ silver nitrate solution is mixed with an excess of potassium bromide solution. Silver bromide is insoluble; potassium nitrate is soluble. Write the balanced equation and calculate the mass of silver bromide precipitate formed ($M(\mathrm{AgBr}) = 188$). (The balanced equation is examinable content; the mass calculation from a concentration in $\mathrm{mol/dm^3}$ is extension, beyond the 0654 syllabus.)
hints: Silver and bromide ions are both singly charged, so check whether any coefficient other than 1 is actually needed.
Use the moles of silver nitrate (the reagent not in excess).
exercises.answer: $\mathrm{AgNO_{3}(aq)} + \mathrm{KBr(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{AgBr(s)} + \mathrm{KNO_{3}(aq)}$. Mass of $\mathrm{AgBr}$ precipitate $= 0.940\,\mathrm{g}$.
exercises.full_solution: All ions here are singly charged, so every coefficient is already 1: left 1 Ag, 1 N, 3 O, 1 K, 1 Br; right 1 Ag, 1 Br, 1 K, 1 N, 3 O. $n(\mathrm{AgNO_{3}}) = 0.125\times0.0400=0.00500\,\mathrm{mol}$; by the 1:1 ratio, $n(\mathrm{AgBr})=0.00500\,\mathrm{mol}$; mass $=0.00500\times188=0.940\,\mathrm{g}$.
common_errors: Forgetting to convert the volume from cm3 to dm3 before substituting into $n=cV$.

exercises.statement: Potassium iodide solution and silver nitrate solution are both colourless. When they are mixed, a pale yellow solid appears immediately. Identify the precipitate, write the balanced symbol equation with state symbols, and describe how a pure, dry sample of it would be isolated from the mixture.
hints: Match the two ions supplied by each solution to work out the formula of the new, insoluble compound.
The isolation procedure is the same three-step method used throughout this lesson, regardless of which specific precipitate is involved.
exercises.answer: The precipitate is silver iodide, $\mathrm{AgI}$. $\mathrm{AgNO_{3}(aq)} + \mathrm{KI(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{AgI(s)} + \mathrm{KNO_{3}(aq)}$. Isolation: filter the mixture (AgI is caught as the residue; the filtrate contains dissolved KNO3 and any excess reagent), wash the residue with a little distilled water, then dry it.
exercises.full_solution: Silver (1+) and iodide (1-) combine 1:1, giving $\mathrm{AgI}$; potassium (1+) and nitrate (1-) combine 1:1, giving $\mathrm{KNO_{3}}$; check: left 1 Ag, 1 N, 3 O, 1 K, 1 I; right 1 Ag, 1 I, 1 K, 1 N, 3 O - balanced with every coefficient equal to 1. The isolation procedure applies the filter/wash/dry method from this lesson directly to a precipitate not explicitly named before.
common_errors: Proposing to evaporate the mixture to obtain the silver iodide, rather than filtering it, since the solid is already present the moment the solutions are mixed.

exercises.statement: $1.70\,\mathrm{g}$ of silver nitrate is dissolved in distilled water and mixed with an excess of potassium bromide solution. Silver bromide is insoluble; potassium nitrate is soluble. ($M(\mathrm{AgNO_{3}}) = 170$, $M(\mathrm{AgBr}) = 188$.) Write the balanced symbol equation, with state symbols, and calculate the mass of silver bromide precipitate formed.
hints: Silver, bromide, potassium and nitrate ions are all singly charged, so check whether any coefficient other than 1 is actually needed.
Find the moles of silver nitrate from its mass using $n = m/M$; it is the reactant that is not in excess, so it fixes the amount of precipitate.
exercises.answer: $\mathrm{AgNO_{3}(aq)} + \mathrm{KBr(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{AgBr(s)} + \mathrm{KNO_{3}(aq)}$. Mass of $\mathrm{AgBr}$ precipitate $= 1.88\,\mathrm{g}$.
exercises.full_solution: Every ion here is singly charged, so all four coefficients are 1: left 1 Ag, 1 N, 3 O, 1 K, 1 Br; right 1 Ag, 1 Br, 1 K, 1 N, 3 O - balanced. $n(\mathrm{AgNO_{3}}) = 1.70/170 = 0.0100\,\mathrm{mol}$. By the 1:1 ratio between $\mathrm{AgNO_{3}}$ and $\mathrm{AgBr}$, $n(\mathrm{AgBr}) = 0.0100\,\mathrm{mol}$, so the mass is $0.0100\times188 = 1.88\,\mathrm{g}$.
common_errors: Multiplying the mass of silver nitrate by its molar mass instead of dividing by it when finding the moles.

exam_questions.statement: $30.0\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of $0.40\,\mathrm{mol/dm^3}$ calcium chloride solution is mixed with an excess of sodium carbonate solution, given that calcium carbonate is insoluble and sodium chloride is soluble. (a) Write the balanced symbol equation, with state symbols. (b) Calculate the mass of calcium carbonate precipitate formed ($M(\mathrm{CaCO_{3}}) = 100$). (c) Describe the three steps needed to obtain this precipitate pure and dry, naming what happens to it at each step. (Part (b) is extension: concentration in $\mathrm{mol/dm^3}$ is beyond the 0654 syllabus. Parts (a) and (c) are the examinable content.)
hints: Use the moles of calcium chloride, not sodium carbonate, since calcium chloride is the reagent that is not in excess.
The three steps follow the general filter/wash/dry method used throughout this lesson.
exam_questions.answer: (a) $\mathrm{CaCl_{2}(aq)} + \mathrm{Na_{2}CO_{3}(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{CaCO_{3}(s)} + 2\mathrm{NaCl(aq)}$. (b) Mass of $\mathrm{CaCO_{3}}$ precipitate $= 1.20\,\mathrm{g}$. (c) Filter the mixture: calcium carbonate is caught on the filter paper as the residue, while the filtrate (dissolved sodium chloride and excess sodium carbonate) passes through. Wash the residue with a little distilled water to remove dissolved by-product from its surface. Dry the washed residue to remove the remaining surface water.
mark_scheme: Correct balanced equation with state symbols (1 mark).
Correct moles of CaCl2, $0.0120\,\mathrm{mol}$ (1 mark).
Correct mass of CaCO3, $1.20\,\mathrm{g}$ (1 mark).
Correctly names filter, wash and dry, each with the correct result (3 marks, 1 each).
common_errors: Describing the final step as 'evaporate the residue', confusing this precipitation procedure with the crystallisation method from the previous lesson.

exam_questions.statement: A student suggests titrating lead(II) nitrate solution against potassium iodide solution, using a colour-change indicator and a burette, in order to make pure lead(II) iodide. Explain two reasons why this approach is not appropriate for preparing this insoluble salt.
hints: One reason concerns what actually signals the reaction is 'finished' in each method.
The other reason concerns why an exact volume match matters in one method but not the other.
exam_questions.answer: Reason 1: lead(II) iodide forms as a visible solid precipitate as soon as enough of both ions are present - there is no indicator colour change relevant to this reaction, since no acid-base neutralisation is taking place. Reason 2: because the product is removed by filtration rather than needing to stay dissolved, there is no need to match the two volumes exactly; in fact, one solution is normally used in deliberate excess, which a titration's exact-volume approach is not designed for.
exam_questions.full_solution: Titration is specifically suited to reactions where the product must remain dissolved and the exact neutralising point matters, signalled by an indicator. Precipitation gives its own visible signal (the solid appearing) and tolerates - indeed benefits from - an excess of one reagent, since the excess simply stays in the filtrate and is removed by filtering and washing, not by precise volume matching.
mark_scheme: States that precipitation has no relevant indicator colour change / no acid-base end point here (1 mark).
States that the solid appears as a visible precipitate on mixing, giving its own signal (1 mark).
States that exact volume matching is unnecessary for precipitation, unlike titration (1 mark).
States that an excess of one reagent is normal and does not harm the final filtered/washed product (1 mark).
common_errors: Arguing only that 'lead(II) iodide is insoluble, so titration can't be used', without explaining what titration actually depends on (an indicator end point and exact volume matching) that makes it unsuitable here.

exam_questions.statement: Pure, dry lead(II) iodide is prepared by precipitation. $3.31\,\mathrm{g}$ of lead(II) nitrate is dissolved in distilled water and mixed with an excess of potassium iodide solution. ($M(\mathrm{Pb(NO_{3})_{2}}) = 331$, $M(\mathrm{PbI_{2}}) = 461$.) (a) Write the balanced symbol equation for the reaction, with state symbols. (b) Calculate the maximum mass of lead(II) iodide that can be formed. (c) State why the potassium iodide is used in excess, and explain why this does not make the dried product impure.
hints: Lead forms a $2+$ ion and iodide is $1-$, so the precipitate needs two iodide ions; balance potassium and nitrate afterwards.
Lead(II) nitrate is the reactant that is not in excess, so its moles fix the amount of precipitate.
exam_questions.answer: (a) $\mathrm{Pb(NO_{3})_{2}(aq)} + 2\mathrm{KI(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{PbI_{2}(s)} + 2\mathrm{KNO_{3}(aq)}$. (b) Maximum mass of $\mathrm{PbI_{2}} = 4.61\,\mathrm{g}$. (c) Excess potassium iodide makes sure that all of the lead(II) nitrate is converted to precipitate, since there is no indicator end point to match the two amounts exactly. It does not spoil the purity of the product because the excess potassium iodide, and the potassium nitrate by-product, both stay dissolved in the filtrate; any trace clinging to the solid is rinsed away when the residue is washed with a little distilled water.
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) Atom check: left 1 Pb, 2 N, 6 O, 2 K, 2 I; right 1 Pb, 2 I, 2 K, 2 N, 6 O - balanced. (b) $n(\mathrm{Pb(NO_{3})_{2}}) = 3.31/331 = 0.0100\,\mathrm{mol}$; by the 1:1 ratio between $\mathrm{Pb(NO_{3})_{2}}$ and $\mathrm{PbI_{2}}$, $n(\mathrm{PbI_{2}}) = 0.0100\,\mathrm{mol}$; mass $= 0.0100\times461 = 4.61\,\mathrm{g}$. (c) The excess reagent and the soluble by-product are both removed at the filtering and washing stages, so only the insoluble lead(II) iodide is left on the paper.
mark_scheme: Correct balanced equation $\mathrm{Pb(NO_{3})_{2}(aq)} + 2\mathrm{KI(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{PbI_{2}(s)} + 2\mathrm{KNO_{3}(aq)}$, with state symbols (1 mark).
Correct moles of lead(II) nitrate, $3.31/331 = 0.0100\,\mathrm{mol}$ (1 mark).
Uses the 1:1 ratio between $\mathrm{Pb(NO_{3})_{2}}$ and $\mathrm{PbI_{2}}$ to give $n(\mathrm{PbI_{2}}) = 0.0100\,\mathrm{mol}$ (1 mark).
Correct mass, $0.0100\times461 = 4.61\,\mathrm{g}$ (1 mark).
States that the excess potassium iodide ensures all the lead(II) nitrate is precipitated (1 mark).
Explains that the excess reagent stays dissolved in the filtrate and is rinsed off by washing the residue, so the dried solid is pure (1 mark).
common_errors: Using a 1:2 ratio between lead(II) nitrate and lead(II) iodide, taking the coefficient 2 in front of KI as though it applied to the precipitate.

challenge_questions.statement:
Pure, dry lead(II) sulfate, $\mathrm{PbSO_{4}}$, is to be prepared by precipitation. The only chemicals available are listed below.

| Compound | Solubility in water |
|---|---|
| lead(II) nitrate | soluble |
| lead(II) sulfate | insoluble |
| lead(II) chloride | insoluble |
| sodium sulfate | soluble |
| sodium nitrate | soluble |
| barium sulfate | insoluble |
| barium nitrate | soluble |

(a) Choose the two solutions that should be mixed, and justify both choices from the data. (b) Write the balanced symbol equation, with state symbols. (c) Explain why neither lead(II) chloride nor barium sulfate can be used as a starting solution, and why mixing barium nitrate with sodium sulfate would not give the required product. (d) Describe how the pure, dry lead(II) sulfate is then obtained.
hints: One solution must supply the $\mathrm{Pb^{2+}}$ ion and the other the $\mathrm{SO_{4}^{2-}}$ ion - and a compound that is insoluble cannot be made into a solution at all.
Check the by-product as well as the product: the compound formed from the two leftover ions must be soluble, or two different solids would end up on the filter paper together.
challenge_questions.answer: (a) Mix lead(II) nitrate solution with sodium sulfate solution. Lead(II) nitrate is the only soluble compound in the list that supplies $\mathrm{Pb^{2+}}$, and sodium sulfate the only soluble one that supplies $\mathrm{SO_{4}^{2-}}$; the leftover sodium and nitrate ions form sodium nitrate, which the data shows is soluble, so it stays dissolved. (b) $\mathrm{Pb(NO_{3})_{2}(aq)} + \mathrm{Na_{2}SO_{4}(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{PbSO_{4}(s)} + 2\mathrm{NaNO_{3}(aq)}$. (c) Lead(II) chloride and barium sulfate are both insoluble, so neither can be dissolved to make a solution that supplies its ions in the first place. Barium nitrate and sodium sulfate would work as a precipitation pair, but neither supplies a lead ion: they would precipitate barium sulfate, a different insoluble salt. (d) Filter the mixture - the lead(II) sulfate is caught on the filter paper as the residue, while the filtrate carries away the dissolved sodium nitrate and any excess reagent. Wash the residue with a little distilled water to rinse off the solution clinging to it, then dry it in a warm oven or between sheets of filter paper.
challenge_questions.full_solution: The choice is forced entirely by the supplied data rather than by any memorised rule. Only two of the listed compounds are both soluble and contain an ion that is needed: lead(II) nitrate for $\mathrm{Pb^{2+}}$ and sodium sulfate for $\mathrm{SO_{4}^{2-}}$. Their by-product, sodium nitrate, is soluble, which is essential - if it were insoluble, two solids would be filtered off together and the product could not be pure. Atom check on the equation: left 1 Pb, 2 N, 6 O from the nitrate groups plus 4 O from the sulfate (10 O in total), 2 Na, 1 S; right 1 Pb, 1 S, 4 O in $\mathrm{PbSO_{4}}$ plus 2 Na, 2 N and 6 O in $2\mathrm{NaNO_{3}}$ - 10 O in total. Balanced. The two rejected starting materials fail for the same single reason: an insoluble compound cannot be supplied as a solution, so its ions are never free in the mixture.
common_errors: Choosing a pair whose by-product is also insoluble, so that two different solids are filtered off together and the product cannot be pure.

mcq.stem: Two soluble solutions are mixed and an insoluble white solid forms. After filtering the mixture, where is this solid found?

options.text: Dissolved in the filtrate.
options.why_wrong: an insoluble solid cannot pass through filter paper and cannot be dissolved in the filtrate; only soluble substances end up in the filtrate.

options.text: Split evenly between the residue and the filtrate.
options.why_wrong: an insoluble solid is entirely caught on the filter paper; none of it passes through into the filtrate.

options.text: On the filter paper, as the residue.
It evaporates away during filtration.
options.why_wrong: filtration is a physical separation, not evaporation; nothing evaporates during this step.

mcq.explanation: An insoluble solid cannot pass through filter paper, so it is entirely retained as the residue; only dissolved substances pass through into the filtrate.

mcq.stem: What is needed to separate an insoluble precipitate from the mixture it formed in?

options.text: Evaporating all of the water away, exactly as for a soluble salt.
options.why_wrong: the precipitate is already a solid as soon as the solutions are mixed; evaporating the water is unnecessary and is not how this method works.

options.text: Titrating with an indicator until the mixture becomes colourless.
options.why_wrong: there is no indicator or colour-change end point involved in a precipitation reaction; the solid simply forms and is then filtered out.

options.text: Cooling the mixture slowly to allow crystals to grow.
options.why_wrong: this describes crystallisation from a concentrated solution, which is how a soluble salt is obtained; a precipitate is already solid and does not need to be grown by cooling.

options.text: Filtering, since the solid is already present the moment the two solutions are mixed.

mcq.explanation: A precipitate is already solid as soon as the two solutions are mixed, so it is separated from the liquid directly by filtering, not by evaporation or cooling.

mcq.stem: Why is precipitation not carried out as a titration?

options.text: Precipitation gives its own visible signal (the solid forming) and does not need an indicator end point or an exact volume match.
Because the two solutions used in precipitation are always insoluble.
options.why_wrong: both solutions used in precipitation are soluble; it is specifically the product that is insoluble, not the starting solutions.

options.text: Because burettes cannot be used to add a solution that will form a precipitate.
options.why_wrong: there is no apparatus limitation preventing a burette from being used; the real reason titration is unsuitable is that there is no indicator end point relevant to a precipitation reaction.

options.text: Because precipitation reactions do not involve measurable amounts of reactants.
options.why_wrong: precipitation reactions can absolutely be measured and calculated with moles, volumes and concentrations, as shown throughout this lesson; this is not the reason titration is unsuitable.

mcq.explanation: Precipitation forms a visible solid directly on mixing, with no indicator colour change to signal an end point, so there is no reason to match volumes exactly as titration requires.

mcq.stem: **Extension (beyond the 0654 syllabus).** $20.0\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of $0.10\,\mathrm{mol/dm^3}$ silver nitrate solution is mixed with excess sodium chloride solution ($M(\mathrm{AgCl}) = 143.5$). What mass of silver chloride precipitate forms?

options.why_wrong: this is 10 times too large, consistent with a power-of-ten slip in the volume (for example, writing 20.0 cm3 as 0.200 dm3 instead of 0.0200 dm3).

this is roughly half the correct mass, consistent with using half the correct number of moles of AgNO3 (for example, mistakenly halving for a 1:2 ratio that does not apply here, since the ratio is 1:1).

this would need 0.0100 mol of AgCl, five times the true amount (for example, from using 0.100 dm3 instead of 0.0200 dm3 for the volume); checking $n=0.10\times0.0200=0.00200\,\mathrm{mol}$ shows the true amount is much smaller.

flashcards.front: What is a precipitate?
flashcards.back: An insoluble solid that forms immediately when two solutions are mixed and their ions combine into a compound that does not dissolve in water.

flashcards.front: How does precipitation differ from crystallisation (the method used for soluble salts)?
flashcards.back: Precipitation forms an insoluble solid immediately on mixing, isolated by filtering, washing and drying, with no evaporation. Crystallisation concentrates a solution of a soluble salt by evaporation and cooling.

flashcards.front: After filtering a precipitation mixture, is the desired insoluble salt in the residue or the filtrate?
flashcards.back: The residue, on the filter paper - an insoluble solid cannot pass through into the filtrate.

flashcards.front: Why is the precipitate washed with distilled water rather than with more of the original solution?
flashcards.back: Distilled water removes soluble by-product solution from the surface of the precipitate without adding any new dissolved substance; the original solution would simply reapply what needs washing off.

flashcards.front: If one reactant solution in a precipitation reaction is deliberately used in excess, which reactant's moles should be used to calculate the mass of precipitate?
flashcards.back: The moles of the reactant that is not in excess (the limiting reagent). In 0654 that amount comes from its mass, using $n = m/M$. (Finding it instead from a volume and a concentration in $\mathrm{mol/dm^3}$, $n = c\times V$, is extension, beyond the syllabus.)

misconceptions.incorrect_model: The insoluble precipitate remains dissolved in the filtrate after filtering, rather than being caught on the filter paper.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Both the residue and the filtrate are described using unfamiliar apparatus vocabulary at the same time, so which one is 'the solid' and which is 'the liquid that passed through' can be swapped by mistake.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner states that the desired insoluble salt is 'in the filtrate' or describes evaporating the filtrate to obtain the precipitate.
misconceptions.correct_model: An insoluble solid cannot pass through filter paper: it is caught on the paper as the residue. The filtrate is the liquid that passes through, and it contains only the soluble by-product(s), dissolved in water, not the precipitate.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask directly: can a solid that does not dissolve in water pass through the tiny holes in filter paper? If a substance is insoluble, it must be the residue, never the filtrate.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: All of the water in the mixture must be evaporated away in order to separate out the insoluble precipitate.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Crystallisation in the previous lesson relied on evaporation, so it is easy to assume every salt-preparation method ends the same way, without noticing that a precipitate is already a solid the moment it forms.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner describes 'evaporating the mixture to dryness' as the method for separating a precipitate, instead of filtering it.
misconceptions.correct_model: A precipitate is already a solid as soon as the two solutions are mixed; no evaporation is needed to form it. It is separated from the liquid immediately by filtering, not by evaporating anything.
misconceptions.remediation: Point out the moment the solid actually appears: it forms the instant the two solutions meet, while still wet, which is completely different from a dissolved salt that only becomes solid once most of its water has been evaporated away.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: An insoluble salt can be obtained by titration, in the same way a soluble salt is made in the previous lesson.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Titration was the headline method of the previous lesson, so it can be over-applied as 'the' method for making any salt, rather than recognised as specific to soluble products made by neutralisation.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner proposes titrating two solutions together, using an indicator and a burette, to make an insoluble salt.
misconceptions.correct_model: Titration measures an exact neutralising volume using an indicator colour change, which only makes sense when the product stays dissolved. Precipitation forms an insoluble solid immediately on mixing, with no indicator end point to look for and no need for an exact volume match; an excess of one solution is normally used simply to make sure as much precipitate as possible forms.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask: does this reaction need an indicator to tell you when to stop adding one solution? A precipitation reaction gives its own, visible signal (the solid appearing) and does not depend on a colour-change end point at all.

common_mistakes.mistake: Describing the precipitate as being in the filtrate.
common_mistakes.why: Unfamiliar apparatus vocabulary (residue, filtrate) can be swapped without a clear physical picture of which one is the solid and which is the liquid.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Ask whether the substance in question is soluble or insoluble: an insoluble solid is always the residue, never the filtrate.

common_mistakes.mistake: Describing the separation method as evaporating the mixture to dryness.
common_mistakes.why: Crystallisation (the previous lesson's method) relies on evaporation, so it can be assumed to apply here as well.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Remember that a precipitate is already a solid the instant the solutions are mixed; the method needed is filtering, not evaporating.

common_mistakes.mistake: Proposing to titrate the two solutions together to make an insoluble salt.
common_mistakes.why: Titration was the headline method of the previous lesson, so it is over-applied to every new salt-preparation situation.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Check whether the product needs to stay dissolved (titration) or is itself insoluble (precipitation, filtered out directly, no indicator needed).

common_mistakes.mistake: Using the volume/concentration of the excess reagent, instead of the limiting reagent, to calculate the mass of precipitate.
common_mistakes.why: Both reagents are given numbers in the question, so it is not always obvious which one is actually limiting.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Identify which reactant is explicitly stated to be 'in excess' first, then use only the other reactant's moles in the calculation.

exam_notes: When asked to describe isolating a precipitate, name all three steps (filter, wash, dry) and state what each one removes or achieves, not just 'filter it'.
A question that states one reagent is 'in excess' is signalling exactly which reagent's moles to use (the other one) in any mass calculation.
When asked why titration is unsuitable for an insoluble product, refer to the lack of an indicator end point and the lack of any need for exact volume matching, not only 'because it's insoluble'.
State symbols matter here: the precipitate is always $(s)$, while the two starting solutions and the soluble by-product are $(aq)$.

summary.big_idea: Mixing two soluble solutions whose ions combine into an insoluble compound produces a precipitate immediately, which is isolated by filtering (as the residue), washing and drying - no evaporation, no indicator, no exact volume match.
key_points: A precipitate forms the instant two solutions supplying the right ions are mixed; no heating or evaporation is needed to make it appear.
The insoluble product is always the residue (caught on filter paper); the filtrate contains only dissolved by-products and any excess reagent.
Isolation is filter, then wash with a little distilled water, then dry - three distinct steps, each removing something different.
Mass-of-precipitate calculations use the moles of the reagent not in excess, the mole ratio from the balanced equation, and the precipitate's molar mass.
Precipitation is not titration: there is no indicator end point and no need to match volumes exactly, so using one reagent in excess is normal, correct technique.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: The insoluble product is the residue, never the filtrate - and it is filtered out the moment it forms, never evaporated.

summary.big_idea: Use the key chemistry ideas and methods from acids bases and salts accurately in mixed practice and exam-style problems.

exercises.statement: Complete the following equations, giving balanced symbol equations: (a) $CH_3COOH + NaOH \rightarrow$ (b) $H_2SO_4 + KOH \rightarrow$ (c) $NH_3 + HBr \rightarrow$. In each case name the acid and the base. Also, for parts (a) and (b), write the ionic equation for the reaction.
exercises.answer: (a) $CH_3COOH(aq) + NaOH(aq) \rightarrow CH_3COONa(aq) + H_2O(l)$ — acid: ethanoic acid (weak acid); base: sodium hydroxide (strong alkali). Ionic equation: $CH_3COOH(aq) + OH^-(aq) \rightarrow CH_3COO^-(aq) + H_2O(l)$. (b) $H_2SO_4(aq) + 2KOH(aq) \rightarrow K_2SO_4(aq) + 2H_2O(l)$ — acid: sulfuric acid (strong acid); base: potassium hydroxide (strong alkali). Ionic equation: $H^+(aq) + OH^-(aq) \rightarrow H_2O(l)$. (c) $NH_3 + HBr \rightarrow NH_4Br$ — acid: hydrogen bromide; base: ammonia (weak base).
exercises.full_solution: Each equation is a simple acid-base (neutralisation) reaction, so the products are a salt plus water (or, for gaseous NH3 + HBr, just the ammonium salt). (a) Ethanoic acid (the acid in vinegar) reacts with sodium hydroxide (the base) to give the salt sodium ethanoate plus water. I balanced it by checking atoms: left-hand side has C2H5O3Na when you add CH3COOH + NaOH, and the right-hand side CH3COONa + H2O also gives C2H5O3Na, so a 1:1:1:1 ratio balances with no extra coefficients needed. For the ionic equation, remember that CH3COOH is a WEAK acid — it only partially ionises in water, so (unlike a strong acid) you do NOT write it as separate H+ and CH3COO- ions on the left. Only the fully-ionised species (NaOH giving Na+ and OH-, with Na+ as a spectator) are split up, so the ionic equation keeps the acid molecule whole: CH3COOH(aq) + OH-(aq) -> CH3COO-(aq) + H2O(l). (b) Sulfuric acid is diprotic (two acidic hydrogens), so it needs two KOH to neutralise it fully: H2SO4 + 2KOH -> K2SO4 + 2H2O. Atom check: both sides have H4 S1 O6 K2, so it balances. Because both H2SO4 and KOH are STRONG and fully ionise in water, the spectator ions (K+ and SO4^2-) cancel out, leaving the standard neutralisation ionic equation H+(aq) + OH-(aq) -> H2O(l). (c) Ammonia gas reacting directly with hydrogen bromide gas is an acid-base reaction without water as a product (it's a gas-phase proton transfer, producing white smoke of solid ammonium bromide): NH3 + HBr -> NH4Br. Atom check: N1 H4 Br1 on both sides, so it balances with no extra coefficients. Ammonia is the base (it accepts a proton to become NH4+); hydrogen bromide is the acid (it donates a proton).

exercises.statement: [[orange:**Extension (beyond the 0654 syllabus): 0654 does not classify acids or alkalis as strong or weak.**]] The table below gives the pH values, in aqueous solution, of several chemicals: potassium hydroxide (pH 13), hydrogen bromide (pH 2), calcium hydroxide (pH 11), sodium chloride (pH 7), hydrogen chloride (pH 2), magnesium hydroxide (pH 10), and citric acid (pH 4). Which of the substances is/are: (a) a strong acid? (b) a weak acid? (c) a strong alkali? (d) a weak alkali? (e) a neutral substance? In each case, write a chemical equation to show the molecules/ions present in solution.
exercises.answer:
(a) Strong acids: hydrogen bromide and hydrogen chloride (pH 2 — fully ionised). (b) Weak acid: citric acid (pH 4 — only partially ionised, so a higher/less extreme pH than the strong acids). (c) Strong alkalis: potassium hydroxide (pH 13) and calcium hydroxide (pH 11) — both dissociate essentially completely. (d) Weak alkali: magnesium hydroxide (pH 10 — only slightly soluble/partially dissociated, giving a markedly lower pH than the strong alkalis). (e) Neutral substance: sodium chloride (pH 7 — a salt of a strong acid and a strong base, so it fully dissociates into spectator ions that do not affect pH). Equations: $HBr(aq) \rightarrow H^+(aq) + Br^-(aq)$; $HCl(aq) \rightarrow H^+(aq) + Cl^-(aq)$; citric acid (weak, written generally as $HA$): $HA(aq) \rightleftharpoons H^+(aq) + A^-(aq)$ (equilibrium lies mostly to the left); $KOH(aq) \rightarrow K^+(aq) + OH^-(aq)$; $Ca(OH)_2(aq) \rightarrow Ca^{2+}(aq) + 2OH^-(aq)$; $Mg(OH)_2(aq) \rightleftharpoons Mg^{2+}(aq) + 2OH^-(aq)$ (equilibrium lies mostly to the left); $NaCl(aq) \rightarrow Na^+(aq) + Cl^-(aq)$.

[[orange:**Note on the 0654 syllabus.**]] This is useful extension practice, but the strong/weak distinction is not part of Cambridge IGCSE Co-ordinated Sciences 0654, which asks only that you compare neutrality, relative acidity and relative alkalinity in terms of colour and pH using universal indicator (C7.1.6). In 0654 you would simply describe pH 2 as strongly acidic, pH 4 as weakly acidic, pH 7 as neutral, pH 10 and pH 11 as weakly alkaline and pH 13 as strongly alkaline - descriptions of the solutions, with no claim about how far each substance ionises. Treat the calcium/magnesium pair with particular care: calcium hydroxide and magnesium hydroxide are both ionic hydroxides, and whatever part of each one dissolves is fully dissociated. The gap between pH 11 and pH 10 here comes from how little of each dissolves - magnesium hydroxide is far less soluble than calcium hydroxide - not from one being 'strong' and the other 'weak'.
exercises.full_solution: The key idea is that pH alone tells you whether something is acidic/alkaline/neutral, but the DEGREE of ionisation (strong vs weak) is read from how extreme the pH is relative to what the substance's concentration would suggest. Strong acids and strong alkalis ionise/dissociate essentially 100% in water, so they push the pH to extreme values (very low for acids, very high for alkalis). Hydrogen bromide and hydrogen chloride are both classic strong acids (full ionisation into H+ and the halide ion), which matches their low pH of 2. Citric acid is a carboxylic acid, and carboxylic acids are weak acids: they only partially ionise, so even though it is acidic, its pH (4) is noticeably higher (less extreme) than the strong acids at the same kind of dilute concentration — I represent this with a reversible arrow, and for simplicity treat it as a generic monoprotic weak acid HA, flagging that citric acid is actually triprotic in reality (three -COOH groups) but GCSE/IGCSE level treats the first ionisation step as representative. Potassium hydroxide and calcium hydroxide are both Group 1/2 hydroxides that are strong bases — they dissociate fully into metal ion and OH-, giving high pH (13 and 11). Calcium hydroxide's pH is a bit lower than potassium hydroxide's mainly because calcium hydroxide is only moderately soluble, so less of it is actually in solution to raise the pH — but whatever does dissolve is still fully dissociated, so it still counts as 'strong' rather than 'weak'. Magnesium hydroxide, by contrast, is only very slightly soluble, so very few hydroxide ions get into solution; its pH (10) is therefore markedly lower than the two strong alkalis, and on the pH scale it is classed as a weak alkali (the dissolved part is shown with a reversible arrow because the solid and its ions are in equilibrium). Sodium chloride is the salt of a strong acid (HCl) and a strong base (NaOH) — in solution it fully dissociates into Na+ and Cl-, but neither ion reacts with water, so the solution stays neutral at pH 7.

exercises.statement: Complete the word equations and write balanced chemical equations for the following soluble salt preparations: (a) magnesium + sulfuric acid $\rightarrow$ (b) calcium carbonate + hydrochloric acid $\rightarrow$ (c) zinc oxide + hydrochloric acid $\rightarrow$ (d) potassium hydroxide + nitric acid $\rightarrow$
exercises.answer: (a) magnesium + sulfuric acid $\rightarrow$ magnesium sulfate + hydrogen: $Mg(s) + H_2SO_4(aq) \rightarrow MgSO_4(aq) + H_2(g)$. (b) calcium carbonate + hydrochloric acid $\rightarrow$ calcium chloride + water + carbon dioxide: $CaCO_3(s) + 2HCl(aq) \rightarrow CaCl_2(aq) + H_2O(l) + CO_2(g)$. (c) zinc oxide + hydrochloric acid $\rightarrow$ zinc chloride + water: $ZnO(s) + 2HCl(aq) \rightarrow ZnCl_2(aq) + H_2O(l)$. (d) potassium hydroxide + nitric acid $\rightarrow$ potassium nitrate + water: $KOH(aq) + HNO_3(aq) \rightarrow KNO_3(aq) + H_2O(l)$.
exercises.full_solution: These are the four standard soluble-salt preparation routes referred to in the chapter: metal + acid, carbonate + acid, (metal) oxide + acid, and alkali + acid. In every case Work out the salt's name by combining the metal (or ammonium) part of the base/carbonate/metal with the acid's anion (sulfate from sulfuric acid, chloride from hydrochloric acid, nitrate from nitric acid), then balanced atom-by-atom. (a) Magnesium (a MAZIT-type moderately reactive metal, safe to react directly with an acid) displaces hydrogen from sulfuric acid: a 1:1:1:1 ratio already balances (Mg1 H2 S1 O4 on both sides). (b) Calcium carbonate reacting with an acid always gives a salt + water + carbon dioxide (a carbonate + acid reaction, distinct from a metal + acid reaction which gives only a salt + hydrogen). Hydrochloric acid has only one acidic hydrogen, but the carbonate ion needs two H+ to be converted to CO2 + H2O, so 2 HCl are needed: this gives Ca1 C1 Cl2 H2 O3 on both sides, confirmed balanced. (c) Zinc oxide is a basic metal oxide, so it neutralises hydrochloric acid the same way a metal hydroxide would — again 2 HCl are needed to supply 2 H+ for the one O2- in ZnO, giving ZnCl2 + H2O (atom check: Zn1 Cl2 H2 O1 both sides). (d) Potassium hydroxide is a strong alkali with a single OH-, which exactly neutralises the single acidic H of nitric acid in a 1:1:1:1 ratio (K1 N1 O4 H2 both sides).

exercises.statement: Lead carbonate and lead iodide are insoluble. Which two soluble salts could you use in the preparation of each substance? Write (a) a word equation (b) a symbol equation (c) an ionic equation to represent the reactions taking place.
exercises.answer: Lead carbonate (precipitation of an insoluble salt): use soluble lead nitrate + soluble sodium carbonate. Word equation: lead nitrate + sodium carbonate $\rightarrow$ lead carbonate + sodium nitrate. Symbol equation: $Pb(NO_3)_2(aq) + Na_2CO_3(aq) \rightarrow PbCO_3(s) + 2NaNO_3(aq)$. Ionic equation: $Pb^{2+}(aq) + CO_3^{2-}(aq) \rightarrow PbCO_3(s)$. Lead iodide: use soluble lead nitrate + soluble potassium iodide. Word equation: lead nitrate + potassium iodide $\rightarrow$ lead iodide + potassium nitrate. Symbol equation: $Pb(NO_3)_2(aq) + 2KI(aq) \rightarrow PbI_2(s) + 2KNO_3(aq)$. Ionic equation: $Pb^{2+}(aq) + 2I^-(aq) \rightarrow PbI_2(s)$.
exercises.full_solution: Because lead carbonate and lead iodide are both insoluble, they cannot be made by the acid + carbonate or acid + metal routes used in Q4 — instead you need DOUBLE DECOMPOSITION (precipitation): mix two different SOLUBLE salts that each supply one of the ions you need (Pb2+ and $\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}$, or Pb2+ and I-), and the insoluble combination precipitates out immediately, leaving the other ions (the 'spectator' nitrate/sodium/potassium ions) in solution. Lead nitrate is the standard soluble source of Pb2+ (almost all nitrates are soluble), so it is the common reagent for both preparations. For the carbonate ion, sodium carbonate is a convenient soluble carbonate; for the iodide ion, potassium iodide is a convenient soluble iodide. I balanced the symbol equations by matching charges: Pb(NO3)2 supplies Pb2+ and 2 NO3-, so it needs a carbonate source that supplies one CO32- to balance the 2+ charge of lead (1:1 ratio with Na2CO3 — Pb1 C1 Na2 N2 O9 both sides), or an iodide source supplying 2 I- (hence 2 KI, not 1), since lead iodide is PbI2 — I verified K1 Pb1 I2 N2 O6 atoms balance both sides. The ionic equations only show the ions that actually combine to form the new insoluble solid; the nitrate, sodium and potassium ions stay dissolved and unchanged, so they are left out as spectator ions.

exercises.statement: An analytical chemist working for an environmental health organisation has been given a sample of water which is thought to have been contaminated by a sulfate, a carbonate and a chloride. (a) Describe how she could confirm the presence of these three types of salt by simple chemical tests. (b) Write ionic equations to help you explain what is happening during the testing process.
exercises.answer: (a) Carbonate: add dilute acid directly to a sample — effervescence occurs and the gas produced turns limewater milky, confirming $\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}$. Sulfate: to a FRESH sample, first acidify with dilute nitric acid (this destroys any carbonate so it cannot interfere), then add aqueous barium nitrate — a white precipitate (barium sulfate) confirms SO4^2-. Chloride: to another fresh sample, acidify with dilute nitric acid (again removing any carbonate), then add aqueous silver nitrate — a white precipitate (silver chloride) confirms Cl-. (b) $CO_3^{2-}(aq) + 2H^+(aq) \rightarrow CO_2(g) + H_2O(l)$; $SO_4^{2-}(aq) + Ba^{2+}(aq) \rightarrow BaSO_4(s)$; $Ag^+(aq) + Cl^-(aq) \rightarrow AgCl(s)$.
exercises.full_solution: This question draws directly on the supplied information (tests for aqueous anions). Treat the three tests as needing SEPARATE portions of the sample, because testing for all three ions in the same portion at the same time would cause interference. The carbonate test is simplest: any dilute acid added to a carbonate releases CO2 gas, visible as bubbling (effervescence), and that gas turns limewater (calcium hydroxide solution) cloudy/milky because it forms insoluble calcium carbonate. For the sulfate and chloride tests, the procedure specifically says to acidify FIRST, before adding barium or silver ions. This is because carbonate ions would also react with Ba2+ (giving insoluble BaCO3) or with Ag+ (giving insoluble Ag2CO3), which would produce a false-positive precipitate that could be mistaken for barium sulfate or silver chloride. Acidifying first converts all the carbonate to CO2 gas, which bubbles out of solution, removing that source of interference, so any precipitate that forms afterwards can only be due to sulfate (with Ba2+) or chloride (with Ag+). The ionic equations show only the ions that combine to form each insoluble precipitate; Checking each one balances in atoms and in charge (e.g. $\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}$ + 2H+ has charge -2+2=0, matching CO2 + H2O which is neutral; SO4^2- + Ba2+ has charge -2+2=0, matching neutral BaSO4; Ag+ + Cl- has charge +1-1=0, matching neutral AgCl).

exercises.statement: For each of the following pairs of substances, describe a chemical test you would carry out to distinguish between them: (a) Ammonium chloride and aluminium chloride. (b) Zinc nitrate and calcium nitrate. (c) Sodium chloride and sodium iodide. (d) Iron(II) sulfate and copper(II) sulfate.
exercises.answer: (a) Add aqueous sodium hydroxide and warm gently: ammonium chloride releases ammonia gas (pungent smell, turns damp red litmus/indicator paper blue) with no permanent precipitate, whereas aluminium chloride gives a white precipitate of Al(OH)3 that DISSOLVES in excess NaOH (amphoteric) to give a colourless solution, with no gas produced. (b) Add aqueous sodium hydroxide, a few drops then excess: both give a white precipitate, but the zinc hydroxide precipitate from zinc nitrate dissolves in excess NaOH to give a colourless solution, whereas the calcium hydroxide precipitate from calcium nitrate is insoluble in excess. (Alternatively, use aqueous ammonia: zinc nitrate gives a white precipitate that dissolves in excess, while calcium nitrate gives no precipitate or only a very slight one.) (c) Acidify each with dilute nitric acid, then add aqueous silver nitrate: sodium chloride gives a white precipitate (AgCl), while sodium iodide gives a yellow precipitate (AgI). (d) Fe2+ solutions are pale green and Cu2+ solutions are blue, so they can be told apart by colour alone; to confirm with a chemical test, add aqueous sodium hydroxide: iron(ii) sulfate gives a green precipitate (Fe(OH)2) that slowly turns rust-brown at the surface on standing in air (oxidation to Fe(OH)3), while copper(II) sulfate gives a blue precipitate (Cu(OH)2) that is insoluble in excess and does not change colour on standing.
exercises.full_solution: Each pair is distinguished by exploiting a different chemical property of one of the two ions present, using NaOH(aq) as the main reagent (consistent with the chapter's 'identifying metal ions' theme) or the halide precipitation test from the supplied information. (a) The key difference is the cation: NH4+ reacts with OH- on warming to release NH3 gas (the only alkaline gas, as the chapter's gas table states), while Al3+ forms a hydroxide precipitate that is amphoteric — it dissolves back into solution in excess NaOH because Al(OH)3 reacts further with OH- to form a soluble aluminate complex ion. (b) Both metal ions form a white hydroxide precipitate with a little NaOH(aq), but zinc hydroxide is amphoteric and dissolves in excess NaOH to give a colourless solution (compare the question's equation ZnO + 2NaOH + H2O -> Na2Zn(OH)4 earlier on this page), while calcium hydroxide stays as a white precipitate, insoluble in excess — this is the result given in the Cambridge qualitative-analysis notes. With aqueous ammonia instead, Ca2+ gives no precipitate (or a very slight one) and Zn2+ gives a white precipitate that dissolves in excess. (c) This extends the supplied information's halide tests: acidifying with dilute nitric acid first removes interference from any carbonate, then Ag+ precipitates each halide with a characteristic colour — white for chloride, cream for bromide (given in the table), and yellow for iodide (the standard extension of this trend, going down Group 7, that is not itself printed in the supplied information but is standard IGCSE knowledge about the silver halides). (d) Iron(II) and copper(II) ions already differ in solution colour, which is often enough, but the more rigorous chemical test is the NaOH precipitate test: Fe(OH)2 is pale green and is unstable in air, oxidising at its surface to rust-brown Fe(OH)3, whereas Cu(OH)2 is a stable blue precipitate that does not change on standing — this visible colour change over time is itself a useful diagnostic feature for Fe2+.

exercises.statement: Sodium carbonate hydrate contains water of crystallisation. When it is heated strongly it gives off the water of crystallisation, which can be collected. The substance left behind is anhydrous sodium carbonate. Describe a chemical test to show that this substance contains sodium (cation) and carbonate (anion).
exercises.answer: Flame test for the sodium cation: dip a clean flame-test (nichrome/platinum) wire into the solid, moisten it, and hold it in a non-luminous Bunsen flame — a persistent yellow/orange flame confirms the presence of sodium ions. Test for the carbonate anion: add a few drops of dilute acid (e.g. dilute hydrochloric acid) to a sample of the solid — effervescence occurs, and if the gas produced is passed into limewater it turns the limewater milky/cloudy white, confirming carbonate ions: $CO_3^{2-} + 2H^+(aq) \rightarrow CO_2(g) + H_2O(l)$ (or, in full, $Na_2CO_3(s) + 2HCl(aq) \rightarrow 2NaCl(aq) + H_2O(l) + CO_2(g)$).
exercises.full_solution: Heating hydrated sodium carbonate removes its water of crystallisation and leaves anhydrous sodium carbonate. Determine the water collected from the change in mass, convert the masses to moles, and use the simplest whole-number ratio to find the number of waters of crystallisation.

exercises.statement: Describe how you would use a combination of sodium hydroxide solution and flame tests to distinguish between different solutions containing the following ions. Explain which tests you would use, in which order you would use them, and what results you would expect to see in each case: (a) $Fe^{2+}$ (b) $Cu^{2+}$ (c) $Li^+$ (d) $Ca^{2+}$ (e) $Fe^{3+}$ (f) $Al^{3+}$ (g) $Mg^{2+}$
exercises.answer:
Do the sodium hydroxide test first, since it separates most of the ions by precipitate colour/behaviour: (a) Fe2+: green precipitate, insoluble in excess, slowly turns rust-brown at the surface on standing in air. (b) Cu2+: blue precipitate, insoluble in excess. (e) Fe3+: red-brown (rust-brown) precipitate, insoluble in excess. (f) Al3+: white precipitate that DISSOLVES in excess NaOH (amphoteric), giving a colourless solution. (c) Li+: NO precipitate forms (lithium hydroxide is soluble). (d) Ca2+ and (g) Mg2+: both give a white precipitate insoluble in excess NaOH, so NaOH alone cannot tell them apart — a flame test is then needed: Ca2+ gives a brick-red/orange-red flame, while Mg2+ gives no characteristic flame colour. A flame test on the Li+ solution (crimson/red flame) can also be used to confirm (c).

[[orange:**Note on the 0654 syllabus.**]] The chemistry above is correct, but parts of it are beyond Cambridge IGCSE Co-ordinated Sciences 0654. The flame tests in 0654 are only lithium (red), sodium (yellow), potassium (lilac) and copper(II) (blue-green), so the brick-red calcium flame is not examined; and the cations tested with aqueous sodium hydroxide and aqueous ammonia are only ammonium, calcium, copper(II), iron(II), iron(III) and zinc, so magnesium and aluminium are not examined either. Inside the syllabus, calcium is identified with no flame test at all: aqueous sodium hydroxide gives a white precipitate that is insoluble in excess, and aqueous ammonia gives no precipitate or only a very slight white precipitate. That second test is what separates $Ca^{2+}$ from $Zn^{2+}$, the other cation in the 0654 list that gives a white precipitate, since the zinc precipitate dissolves in an excess of either reagent to give a colourless solution.
exercises.full_solution: The NaOH(aq) test exploits the fact that most transition-metal and group 2/3 hydroxides are insoluble and often coloured, while group 1 hydroxides (like LiOH) are soluble — so Use it as the first, quick screening test, then reserved flame tests only for the cases NaOH cannot resolve on its own. Running through the ions: Fe2+ and Fe3+ give differently-coloured hydroxide precipitates (green vs red-brown) that are both insoluble in excess NaOH, so they are each uniquely identified by colour alone. Cu2+ gives a blue precipitate, also insoluble in excess, giving it a unique identity too. Al3+ is the one precipitate among this set that is amphoteric — it initially looks like a white precipitate (similar to Mg2+ or Ca2+) but, unlike them, it visibly dissolves back into solution when excess NaOH is added, which is the diagnostic step that separates it from Mg2+/Ca2+. Li+ is the odd one out because Group 1 hydroxides are soluble, so no precipitate at all forms with NaOH — this alone identifies Li+ among this set, since it is the only ion with no precipitate whatsoever. That leaves Ca2+ and Mg2+, which both give a white precipitate that does not redissolve in excess NaOH, so the NaOH test cannot distinguish this pair — I therefore use a flame test as the second, confirmatory test specifically for this pair (and optionally to double-check Li+): Ca2+ gives the characteristic brick-red/orange-red flame of Group 2 calcium compounds, whereas Mg2+ does not give a distinctive flame colour at all (magnesium is not normally included in standard flame-test colour tables for this reason), so the presence or absence of a brick-red flame cleanly separates Ca2+ from Mg2+.

exercises.statement: Name the substances A to E shown in the flow diagram. Iron reacts via two routes: (route 1) iron + chlorine + heat $\rightarrow$ solid A; solid A dissolved in water, then aqueous sodium hydroxide added $\rightarrow$ rust-brown precipitate D. (route 2) iron + dilute hydrochloric acid $\rightarrow$ solution B + gas C; solution B + aqueous silver nitrate $\rightarrow$ white precipitate E. Identify: (a) Solid A (b) Solution B (c) Gas C (d) Rust-brown precipitate D (e) White precipitate E.
exercises.answer: (a) Solid A = iron(iii) chloride, $FeCl_3$ (iron burning in chlorine is oxidised fully to the +3 state): $2Fe(s) + 3Cl_2(g) \rightarrow 2FeCl_3(s)$. (b) Solution B = iron(ii) chloride, $FeCl_2(aq)$ (iron reacting with dilute acid only reaches the +2 state): $Fe(s) + 2HCl(aq) \rightarrow FeCl_2(aq) + H_2(g)$. (c) Gas C = hydrogen, $H_2$. (d) Rust-brown precipitate D = iron(iii) hydroxide, $Fe(OH)_3(s)$: $FeCl_3(aq) + 3NaOH(aq) \rightarrow Fe(OH)_3(s) + 3NaCl(aq)$. (e) White precipitate E = silver chloride, $AgCl(s)$: $FeCl_2(aq) + 2AgNO_3(aq) \rightarrow 2AgCl(s) + Fe(NO_3)_2(aq)$, ionic equation $Ag^+(aq) + Cl^-(aq) \rightarrow AgCl(s)$.
exercises.full_solution: The crucial chemical idea linking the two routes is that iron can show two different oxidation states (+2 or +3) depending on how vigorously it is oxidised. Burning iron directly in chlorine gas with heat is a strong oxidising environment, so iron is oxidised all the way to iron(iii) chloride (A); I balanced this as 2Fe + 3Cl2 -> 2FeCl3, confirmed Fe2 Cl6 on both sides. Dissolving solid A in water simply gives Fe3+(aq) and Cl-(aq) ions, and adding NaOH(aq) precipitates the characteristic rust-brown iron(iii) hydroxide (D), using the same equation already verified in this chapter's text (FeCl3 + 3NaOH -> Fe(OH)3 + 3NaCl, atoms balance Fe1 Cl3 Na3 O3 H3 both sides). By contrast, dilute hydrochloric acid is a much weaker oxidant (really, it's just an acid reacting with a metal, releasing hydrogen rather than oxidising iron strongly), so this route only produces iron(ii) chloride (B) plus hydrogen gas (C) — exactly matching the metal + acid pattern described earlier in the chapter (hydrogen ions gain electrons from the metal to form H2 gas): Fe + 2HCl -> FeCl2 + H2, atom check Fe1 Cl2 H2 both sides. Finally, solution B (containing Cl- ions, since it's iron(ii) CHLORIDE) reacts with silver nitrate in the classic halide test from the supplied information: Ag+ + Cl- -> AgCl(s), giving the white precipitate E. Use this chloride-ion response specifically to confirm that B must be a chloride (ruling out, for example, iron(ii) nitrate, which would give no precipitate with AgNO3).

exercises.statement: Describe how you would use simple test-tube reactions to distinguish between the following pairs of ions. In each case describe the test and its result: (a) $Fe^{2+}$ and $Fe^{3+}$ (b) $CO_3^{2-}$ and $Cl^-$ (c) $Ca^{2+}$ and $Zn^{2+}$ (d) $Fe^{3+}$ and $Al^{3+}$ (e) $Mg^{2+}$ and $NH_4^+$
exercises.answer: (a) Add aqueous NaOH: Fe2+ gives a green precipitate (Fe(OH)2), Fe3+ gives a red-brown/rust-brown precipitate (Fe(OH)3) — both are insoluble in excess, so colour alone distinguishes them. (b) Add dilute acid (e.g. dilute nitric acid): carbonate gives effervescence (CO2 gas, turns limewater milky), chloride gives no visible reaction. (c) Add aqueous NaOH, then excess: both give a white precipitate, but the zinc precipitate DISSOLVES in excess (amphoteric) to give a colourless solution, while the calcium precipitate is insoluble in excess. (With aqueous ammonia, zinc gives a white precipitate soluble in excess and calcium gives no precipitate or only a very slight one.) (d) Add aqueous NaOH: iron(iii) gives a red-brown precipitate insoluble in excess, aluminium gives a white precipitate that DISSOLVES in excess (amphoteric) to give a colourless solution. (e) Add aqueous NaOH and warm: magnesium gives a white precipitate insoluble in excess with no gas evolved; ammonium gives no precipitate but releases ammonia gas (pungent smell, turns damp red litmus/indicator paper blue).
exercises.full_solution: Each pair is separated by a property that one ion has and the other does not, mostly using the sodium hydroxide precipitation test built up earlier in the chapter (and reused in Q10), plus the carbonate acid test from the supplied information for part (b). (a) Fe2+ and Fe3+ hydroxides are both insoluble in excess NaOH but have very different colours (green vs red-brown), so a single NaOH test is enough. (b) This reuses the standard carbonate test: only $\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}$ reacts with acid to release CO2 gas (confirmed via limewater); Cl- is simply unreactive with dilute acid, so the absence of effervescence confirms chloride. (c) This is the same contrast used in Q8(b): both ions give a white hydroxide precipitate with NaOH(aq), but Zn(OH)2 is amphoteric and redissolves in excess NaOH, while Ca(OH)2 stays as a white precipitate, insoluble in excess. (d) This reuses the Al3+ amphoteric behaviour from Q10: Fe(OH)3 stays as a red-brown solid in excess NaOH, while Al(OH)3, despite initially looking similar (a white solid), dissolves in excess NaOH because aluminium hydroxide is amphoteric. (e) The key difference here is that NH4+ is NOT a metal ion at all — warming it with NaOH releases ammonia gas (detectable by smell and by turning damp red litmus/indicator paper blue, as given in the chapter's gas table), whereas Mg2+ simply forms an insoluble white hydroxide precipitate with no gas produced. This gas-vs-precipitate contrast is the standard way to distinguish an ammonium salt from a genuine metal salt.
