exercises.statement: Use the words and formulae below to complete the following passage about limestone and its uses. Word bank: CaO, building, CaCO3, acids, thermal, CO2, oxide, acidity, quarries, quicklime, calcium. 'Limestone is a very common rock. The main chemical in limestone is _____ carbonate (chemical formula, _____ ). Limestone is obtained from _____ . The uses of limestone are many and varied. For example, because it is easy to cut into blocks it is useful as a _____ material. Also it will react with _____ and so it is used in the powder form to reduce soil _____ . When limestone is heated very strongly, it breaks down into _____ (chemical name, calcium _____ ) and carbon dioxide (chemical formula, _____ ). This kind of reaction is known as _____ decomposition.'
exercises.answer: 'Limestone is a very common rock. The main chemical in limestone is calcium carbonate (chemical formula, CaCO3). Limestone is obtained from quarries. The uses of limestone are many and varied. For example, because it is easy to cut into blocks it is useful as a building material. Also it will react with acids and so it is used in the powder form to reduce soil acidity. When limestone is heated very strongly, it breaks down into quicklime (chemical name, calcium oxide) and carbon dioxide (chemical formula, CO2). This kind of reaction is known as thermal decomposition.'
exercises.full_solution: I worked through the passage blank by blank, matching each gap to a word from the bank by its grammatical role and chemical meaning. 'Calcium' fits the first gap ('_____ carbonate') since limestone's main component is calcium carbonate, and its formula is CaCO3, which fills the second gap. Limestone rock is physically extracted from 'quarries' (an open-pit mining site for rock), filling the third gap. Because limestone blocks are easy to cut, it is traditionally used as a 'building' material. Limestone (being calcium carbonate, a base/weak alkali-reacting compound) reacts with 'acids', which is exactly why powdered limestone is spread on fields to reduce soil 'acidity' (this matches the main text on this very page, about spreading limestone on soil). Finally, strongly heating limestone causes it to THERMALLY decompose (named explicitly as 'thermal decomposition' in the final gap) into 'quicklime' (the common/trade name for the product) which is chemically calcium 'oxide' (CaO), plus carbon dioxide, whose formula is 'CO2'. Note that the word bank contains 11 words but the passage only has 10 blanks — 'CaO' is left unused, because the passage specifically asks for the chemical NAME of the solid product ('calcium _____') rather than its formula at that point (the formula was already supplied separately for CO2, and calcium carbonate's formula CaCO3 was asked for explicitly elsewhere), so CaO is simply a distractor word in this cloze exercise and does not indicate any error.

exercises.statement: Lime is a very important substance. For example it is a base. It is also used in flue gas desulfurisation. (a) What do you understand by the term base? (b) Which gas is the main gas removed by flue gas desulfurisation? (c) Name a gas you have studied which can be dried using lime.
exercises.answer: (a) A base is a substance (typically a metal oxide, metal hydroxide, or ammonia) that reacts with an acid to form only a salt and water (a neutralisation reaction); a base that dissolves in water is also called an alkali. (b) Sulfur dioxide, $SO_2$ ('desulfurisation' literally means removing sulfur-containing gas from the flue/exhaust gases). (c) Ammonia, $NH_3$ — lime (CaO) is a basic/alkaline solid drying agent, so it is suitable for drying a basic gas like ammonia (an acidic drying agent such as concentrated sulfuric acid would react with and neutralise ammonia instead of just drying it).
exercises.full_solution: (a) This is a definitional/recall question: the chapter defines a base operationally by what it does chemically — it neutralises an acid, producing a salt and water as the only products (this is the same neutralisation idea used throughout the earlier acids-and-salts pages, e.g. $HCl + NaOH \rightarrow NaCl + H_2O$). An alkali is simply the special case of a soluble base. (b) 'Flue gas desulfurisation' is a named industrial process whose purpose, as the name states, is to remove sulfur-containing pollutant gas (sulfur dioxide, produced when sulfur impurities in fossil fuels burn) from the waste ('flue') gases of power stations, using a base like calcium oxide or calcium carbonate to neutralise/absorb the acidic SO2 before it is released and causes acid rain. (c) A drying agent must not react with the gas it is drying. Lime (CaO) is itself basic/alkaline, so it cannot be used to dry an acidic gas (like CO2 or HCl) or even be fully safe with some neutral gases, but it is the standard solid drying agent for a basic gas — and the only basic gas studied in this chapter (as stated directly in the supplied information, 'it is the only alkaline gas') is ammonia, NH3. Using an acidic drying agent (such as concentrated sulfuric acid, normally used for many other gases) on ammonia would be unsuitable, since the acid would react with and neutralise the ammonia instead of simply drying it — which is exactly why a basic drying agent like lime is needed here.
